gaps: No create-level activities: Students never design complete solutions, propose new architectures, or synthesize novel structures. For MSc-level, at least one activity asking students to design a simple class hierarchy or propose a quality-focused refactoring would be appropriate.

Slides 5-8 (individual quality attributes) remain purely explanatory without application activities. Students could benefit from analyzing code snippets to identify which attributes are violated or applying attributes to evaluate simple design alternatives.

Slides 11-13 (classes, objects, encapsulation) are entirely passive. Adding a brief activity where students sketch a class design for a familiar domain (e.g., university course enrollment) would move from understanding to application.

Limited synthesis across concepts: While individual topics reach analyze/evaluate levels, no activity asks students to integrate multiple concepts (e.g., design a class that balances all four quality attributes, or evaluate how encapsulation specifically supports extendibility in a given design).
suggestions: Add create-level capstone activity: After Slide 16, include a 5-minute activity where students design a simple class (e.g., LIBRARY_BOOK with checkout/return operations) that demonstrates all four quality attributes and proper encapsulation. This synthesizes the lecture's concepts.

Enhance Slides 5-8 with mini-activities: After defining each quality attribute, provide a 30-second code snippet and ask students to identify violations. Example for Slide 5 (Correctness): Show a sorting function that works for positive numbers but fails for negatives—students identify the specification gap.

Convert Slide 13 (Encapsulation) to apply level: Add activity where students are given a poorly encapsulated class (public attributes, no validation) and sketch how to refactor it with proper encapsulation, identifying which quality attributes improve.

Strengthen integration in Slide 9: Current activity evaluates trade-offs well, but could ask students to also propose one specific design decision for each system that reflects the prioritization (e.g., 'For medical device, how would you structure update mechanisms to prioritize correctness?').

Add metacognitive reflection: Include a final slide asking students to self-assess which Bloom level they reached for each objective and identify one concept they need to practice at a higher level. This develops self-regulated learning.

Balance passive slides: Slides 11-13 are consecutive explanation slides. Insert a brief pair-share after Slide 12 where students explain class-object relationship to each other using a non-computing analogy (recipe-dish, blueprint-building), then share analogies with class to check understanding.

slides.title: Introduction to Software Engineering and Object-Oriented Fundamentals

blocks.content: Lecture 1: Introduction to Software Engineering and Object-Oriented Fundamentals
Software Construction, Architecture and Engineering

content.title: Analyze: Your Software Engineering Experience
content.instructions: Reflect on a software project you've worked on. Identify one concrete example where the code worked correctly but was difficult to modify or reuse. What made it problematic? Write down the specific issue (tight coupling, unclear structure, hardcoded values, etc.).
content.purpose: Activate prior knowledge; diagnose gap between 'working code' and 'engineered systems'

slides.speakerNotes: Welcome students warmly. Launch the reflection activity immediately to activate prior experience and surface the central problem this course addresses: code that works isn't enough. After 2 minutes, ask 2-3 volunteers to share examples. Listen for themes like 'couldn't change X without breaking Y' or 'copy-pasted code everywhere.' Use their responses to preview that this course provides systematic principles (quality attributes, OO design) to prevent these problems. This diagnostic helps students see why engineering discipline matters beyond basic programming competence.

slides.title: Course Structure and Objectives

blocks.content: Your Learning Journey

items: Three pillars: Construction (correctness), Architecture (structure), Engineering (long-term quality)
35h lectures + 35h tutorials + 55h independent study
Assessment: 50% written exam + 50% portfolio demonstrating pillar integration
Eiffel notation → transferable OO principles for any language

content.title: Evaluate & Create: Diagnose and Redesign
content.instructions: Select a past project. (1) Evaluate it against all three pillars using a 1-5 scale for each. (2) Identify your weakest pillar. (3) Propose one concrete improvement that would strengthen that pillar (e.g., 'Add input validation for Construction' or 'Extract reusable modules for Architecture'). Share your proposal with a neighbor and explain why it addresses the gap.
content.purpose: Self-assess learning needs; create actionable improvement linked to course pillars

slides.speakerNotes: Present the three-pillar framework with brief examples: Construction ensures correctness through contracts, Architecture organizes complexity via modularity, Engineering sustains quality over decades through reusability and extendibility. Launch the activity to make pillars diagnostic and actionable. Circulate during pair discussions, listening for whether students grasp pillar distinctions. Debrief by collecting 2-3 proposed improvements and highlighting how the course provides systematic techniques for each. Emphasize that portfolio assessment rewards demonstrating growth across all pillars, not just producing working code. This activity raises cognitive demand to evaluate (self-assess against criteria) and create (propose targeted solution).

slides.title: The Software Engineering Challenge

blocks.content: Why Software Engineering Matters

items: Modern systems: millions of lines, decades of evolution
Industrial software ≠ academic exercises
Ad-hoc approaches fail at scale → systematic methods required
Example: Ariane 5 ($500M loss from reused code without analysis)

content.title: Analyze & Diagnose: From Failure to Principle
content.instructions: Read: Ariane 5 reused Ariane 4 altitude code. The new rocket's faster acceleration caused integer overflow, triggering self-destruct 37 seconds after launch. Which quality attribute(s) were violated? What engineering practice would have prevented this? Discuss with a neighbor, then propose one specific verification step the team should have performed.
content.purpose: Apply quality attributes to analyze real failure; connect abstract principles to concrete engineering practices

slides.speakerNotes: Present the Ariane 5 case as a concrete failure illustrating why systematic engineering matters. Launch the activity to move students from passively hearing the story to actively diagnosing it using quality concepts. Expected answers: robustness violated (didn't handle unexpected input range), extendibility violated (reuse without adaptation). Prevention: specification analysis, range testing, contracts. Debrief by collecting proposed verification steps, highlighting that engineering discipline means validating assumptions during reuse. This raises cognitive demand to analyze (diagnose root cause) and apply (map failure to quality framework), preparing students for the detailed quality attributes in Slide 4.

slides.title: Quality Attributes: The Foundation

blocks.content: Four Pillars of Software Quality

items: Correctness: Does it do what it should?
Robustness: Does it handle the unexpected?
Extendibility: Can it adapt to change?
Reusability: Can we leverage it elsewhere?

content.title: Diagnose, Classify & Propose Solutions
content.instructions: Online banking system scenarios: (1) Transfer moves $99 instead of $100. (2) System crashes on text in amount field. (3) Adding crypto requires rewriting transaction code. (4) Authentication can't be reused in mobile app. First, classify which quality attribute each violates. Then, propose one concrete design decision or practice that would prevent scenario (3). Share your solution with a neighbor and refine it together.
content.deliverable: Classification + one specific prevention strategy for extendibility failure

slides.speakerNotes: After introducing the four attributes, launch the activity. Give 90 seconds for individual classification and solution proposal, then 90 seconds pair discussion to refine prevention strategies, finally 60 seconds class debrief. Expected classifications: (1) correctness, (2) robustness, (3) extendibility, (4) reusability. For scenario 3, look for answers like 'use abstract payment interface' or 'separate transaction logic from payment method.' This elevates from pure classification to proposing preventive design decisions, bridging analysis to evaluation/creation. Highlight that quality attributes guide concrete architectural choices, preparing students for deeper attribute exploration in subsequent slides.

slides.title: Correctness: Doing the Right Thing

blocks.content: Correctness

items: Performs exact tasks as specified
Binary property: correct or incorrect
Requires clear, formal specifications
Most fundamental quality attribute

content.title: Identify Correctness Violations
content.instructions: Analyze this code snippet: A sort_list function specification states 'Sort integers in ascending order.' Implementation uses bubble sort but has condition: if (list[i] > list[i+1]) swap(). Which input reveals incorrectness? (A) [3,1,2] (B) [-5,3,-1] (C) [1,2,3] (D) All work correctly. Identify the answer and explain why it violates the specification.
content.deliverable: Answer selection with one-sentence justification

slides.speakerNotes: Launch activity immediately after defining correctness. Answer is D—the code is actually correct for the specification. This challenges students to analyze specification-implementation alignment rather than just spotting bugs. After polling, reveal answer and emphasize that correctness requires complete specification coverage. If time permits, modify scenario: change spec to 'Sort all numbers' but keep integer-only implementation—now inputs with floats reveal incorrectness. Connect to next slide: correctness assumes valid inputs; invalid inputs relate to robustness.

slides.title: Robustness: Handling the Unexpected

blocks.content: Robustness

items: Graceful response to abnormal conditions
Complements correctness (exceptional vs. normal cases)
Error handling and exception management
Fail-safe design: maintain safety under failure

content.title: Diagnose Robustness Failures
content.instructions: Analyze these two implementations of withdraw(amount) for a bank account: (A) Subtracts amount from balance without checks. (B) Checks if amount > balance, displays 'Error: Insufficient funds' and prevents withdrawal. For each scenario, identify which implementation fails robustness and explain what abnormal condition is mishandled: (1) User enters -50 as amount (2) Database connection drops mid-withdrawal (3) User enters 'abc' as amount. Propose one improvement for the most critical gap.
content.deliverable: Identify failure cases and propose one robustness enhancement

slides.speakerNotes: Launch activity after defining robustness. Both implementations have robustness gaps: (A) fails all scenarios; (B) handles overdraft but not negative inputs, connection failures, or type errors. Critical gap is transaction consistency (scenario 2). Students should recognize robustness requires anticipating multiple abnormal conditions beyond obvious cases. After pairs discuss, poll for most critical gap and collect improvement proposals (e.g., transaction rollback, input validation). Connect to extendibility: robust error handling structures affect how easily we add new validations later.

slides.title: Extendibility: Embracing Change

blocks.content: Extendibility

items: Ease of adapting to specification changes
Change is inevitable in software
Modular design and separation of concerns
Localized changes vs. ripple effects
Design for change from day one

content.prompt: Side-by-side comparison showing two system architectures. Left side (Good): modular boxes with one highlighted in red showing localized change, other modules unaffected. Right side (Poor): tangled web of dependencies with one change in red causing ripple effects (shown in orange) throughout system. Label: 'Well-designed vs. Poorly-designed System Response to Change'

slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize that requirements always change - new features, regulatory updates, business pivots. Example: e-commerce system adding cryptocurrency payment without restructuring entire checkout. Good design localizes changes: adding new payment method shouldn't require modifying inventory management. Mention the Open-Closed Principle preview: open for extension, closed for modification. Poor extendibility leads to maintenance nightmares and eventual system rewrites. Object-oriented mechanisms like inheritance and polymorphism support extendibility.

slides.title: Reusability: Leveraging Existing Solutions

blocks.content: Reusability

items: Using software elements across multiple applications
Economic benefits: reduced time and cost
Libraries, frameworks, and components
Trade-off: generality vs. specificity
Requires upfront design investment

content.prompt: Pyramid diagram showing reusability spectrum. Base (widest): 'Widely Reusable Libraries' (e.g., data structures, math). Middle: 'Domain-Specific Frameworks' (e.g., web, games). Top (narrowest): 'Application-Specific Code'. Arrows showing decreasing reusability upward, increasing specialization upward.

slides.speakerNotes: Highlight economic impact: reusable components dramatically reduce development time. Example: standard library collections (List, Set, Map) used in millions of applications - imagine if every project reimplemented these! Discuss the reusability spectrum: highly general (math libraries) to domain-specific (authentication modules) to application-specific. Note the paradox: making something reusable requires more effort upfront (generalization, documentation, testing) but pays dividends across projects. Object-oriented features like inheritance and generics enable reusability.

slides.title: Quality Attributes: Trade-offs in Practice

blocks.content: Analyzing Quality Attribute Trade-offs

Three systems with different priorities: (A) Medical device firmware—safety-critical, infrequent updates. (B) E-commerce platform—frequent feature additions, third-party integrations. (C) Scientific computation library—used across multiple research domains.

content.title: Evaluate & Propose (5 min)
content.instructions: For each system, rank the four quality attributes by priority AND propose one concrete design decision that reflects your ranking. Example: 'Medical device prioritizes correctness, so I'd require formal verification of all updates before deployment.' Think individually (1.5 min), discuss with neighbor (2.5 min), share one proposal (1 min).
content.deliverable: Ranking + specific design decision for at least one system

items: Medical: Correctness/Robustness > Extendibility (formal methods, extensive testing, update restrictions)
E-commerce: Extendibility > Performance (plugin architecture, API versioning, feature flags)
Library: Reusability/Correctness > Specificity (generic interfaces, comprehensive test suites)
Trade-offs require explicit design choices—not just priorities

slides.speakerNotes: This enhanced activity pushes students from evaluation to creation by requiring concrete design proposals. After pair discussions, solicit 2-3 design decisions per system and probe how they operationalize priorities. Highlight examples: medical devices might use immutable data structures (correctness), e-commerce might adopt microservices (extendibility), libraries might use abstract base classes (reusability). Emphasize that recognizing trade-offs is insufficient—engineers must translate priorities into architectural choices. Preview that OO mechanisms (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism) provide systematic tools for implementing these decisions, which upcoming slides will explore.

slides.title: Why Object-Oriented Programming?

blocks.content: Evaluating OO vs. Procedural Approaches

Scenario: Library management system tracking books, members, and loans. Two designs: (A) Procedural—separate data files (books.dat, members.dat) with functions process_loan(), calculate_fine(), update_inventory(). (B) Object-Oriented—classes BOOK, MEMBER, LOAN with encapsulated data and methods.

content.title: Design Evaluation (4 min)
content.instructions: Compare both designs against our four quality attributes. Which approach better supports correctness, robustness, extendibility, and reusability? Identify one specific advantage OO provides. Think individually (1 min), discuss with neighbor (2 min), share verdict (1 min).
content.deliverable: Justify your choice: which design would you recommend and why?

items: OO: Encapsulation protects invariants (correctness/robustness)
OO: Adding late fee policy modifies LOAN class only (extendibility)
Procedural: Changes ripple across multiple functions
OO: MEMBER class reusable in other university systems (reusability)

slides.speakerNotes: This evaluate-level activity asks students to critically assess design paradigms rather than passively accepting OO superiority. After pair discussions, poll the room and probe reasoning. Highlight that procedural design scatters related logic (loan processing touches multiple files/functions), making changes risky. OO localizes changes: adding email notifications affects MEMBER class only. Emphasize encapsulation's role: BOOK ensures valid ISBN, LOAN enforces return dates—invariants protected by design. Connect back to Slide 9's trade-offs: OO systematically supports quality attributes through structural mechanisms, not just conventions.

slides.title: Classes: Blueprints for Objects

blocks.content: Classes

items: Template defining structure and behavior
Attributes (data) and methods (operations)
Class as a type in the type system
Abstract data type with hidden implementation
Unit of modularity and reuse

content.prompt: UML class diagram showing BANK_ACCOUNT class. Top section: class name 'BANK_ACCOUNT'. Middle section (attributes): '- balance: REAL', '- account_number: STRING'. Bottom section (methods): '+ deposit(amount: REAL)', '+ withdraw(amount: REAL)', '+ get_balance(): REAL'. Use standard UML notation with minus for private, plus for public.

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce class as fundamental OO concept: a blueprint or template. Analogy: architectural blueprint defines structure of houses, class defines structure of objects. Class contains attributes (data, state) and methods (operations, behavior). Example: BANK_ACCOUNT class defines what it means to be a bank account - every account has balance and account number, supports deposit and withdraw. Class is also a type: variables can be declared of class type. Emphasize that class is abstract - it's a definition, not a concrete entity (that's an object).

slides.title: Objects: Runtime Instances

blocks.content: Objects

items: Runtime instance of a class
Each object has unique identity
Object state: current attribute values
Lifecycle: creation, use, destruction
Multiple objects from same class

content.prompt: Object diagram showing three BANK_ACCOUNT instances. Top: BANK_ACCOUNT class box. Below, three object boxes connected to class with dashed arrows: 'alice_account' (balance: 1000.0, account_number: 'A001'), 'bob_account' (balance: 2500.0, account_number: 'B002'), 'carol_account' (balance: 500.0, account_number: 'C003'). Label: 'Class and its Instances'

slides.speakerNotes: Distinguish class (abstract template) from object (concrete instance). Analogy: blueprint vs. actual houses built from it. Each object has identity (alice_account ≠ bob_account even if they have same balance), state (current values of all attributes), and behavior (responds to method calls). Objects are created at runtime, exist in memory, and eventually destroyed. Multiple objects can be created from same class, each with different state. Example: three bank accounts for Alice, Bob, Carol - all instances of BANK_ACCOUNT but with different balances and account numbers.

slides.title: Encapsulation: Information Hiding

blocks.content: Encapsulation

items: Bundling data with operations
Separating interface from implementation
Public interface vs. private details
Access control: public, private, protected
Benefits: reduced coupling, easier maintenance

content.prompt: Conceptual diagram of an object as a circle with thick boundary. Inside (private): 'balance: 1000.0', 'internal_state', 'implementation details'. Outside boundary (public interface): arrows pointing to 'deposit()', 'withdraw()', 'get_balance()'. External clients shown as small boxes outside, accessing only through public interface. Label: 'Encapsulation Boundary'

slides.speakerNotes: Encapsulation is crucial for quality: it's the mechanism that enables extendibility and reusability. Two aspects: (1) bundling data with operations that manipulate it, (2) hiding implementation details. Example: BANK_ACCOUNT balance is private - clients can't directly modify it, must use deposit/withdraw methods. This enforces invariants (balance never goes negative) and allows implementation changes (store balance in cents vs. dollars) without affecting clients. Analogy: car dashboard (public interface) vs. engine internals (private implementation). Encapsulation reduces coupling between components.

slides.title: Introduction to Eiffel

blocks.content: Eiffel: A Language for Quality Software

items: Designed specifically for software engineering principles
Strong support for Design by Contract
Clear, readable syntax emphasizing concepts over tricks
Advanced features: inheritance, genericity, multiple inheritance

content.title: Analyze: Language Choice Trade-offs
content.instructions: Consider these two scenarios: (1) Teaching software quality principles to MSc students, (2) Building a commercial web application. In pairs, analyze which language characteristics matter most for each scenario and justify whether Eiffel or a mainstream language (Java/Python) better serves each purpose. Focus on how language features support or hinder the four quality attributes.

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce Eiffel and address 'Why not Java/Python?' Answer: Eiffel was designed by Bertrand Meyer specifically to teach software engineering principles with clean syntax emphasizing concepts. Design by Contract is built-in. The activity asks students to analyze trade-offs between pedagogical clarity and industry adoption, connecting language features to quality attributes from earlier slides. This develops critical evaluation skills: recognizing that tool choice depends on context and priorities. Debrief by emphasizing concept transferability—principles learned in Eiffel apply everywhere, like learning music theory on piano helps with any instrument.

slides.title: Eiffel Class Structure

content.code:
class POINT
create make
feature {NONE} -- Initialization
    make (a_x, a_y: REAL)
        do
            x := a_x
            y := a_y
        end
feature -- Access
    x: REAL
    y: REAL
feature -- Measurement
    distance_to (other: POINT): REAL
        do
            Result := sqrt((x - other.x)^2 + (y - other.y)^2)
        end
end

content.title: Create: Design CIRCLE Class
content.instructions: Design a complete CIRCLE class with center (POINT), radius (REAL), and operations: make, area, contains (tests if a point is inside). Sketch the class structure showing: (1) Which features are public/private and why, (2) How your design supports correctness and encapsulation, (3) One precondition that prevents misuse. Share your design rationale with a neighbor, focusing on which quality attributes your decisions prioritize.

slides.speakerNotes: Walk through POINT syntax: class/create clauses, feature grouping, attributes versus methods, Result keyword, assignment operator. Emphasize feature {NONE} for private initialization. Launch activity: students synthesize a complete class design from scratch, integrating syntax patterns with quality principles from earlier slides. This elevates from applying a single pattern to creating a cohesive design. During debrief, collect designs on board showing different encapsulation choices (is radius public?), preconditions (radius > 0 in make), and how decisions reflect quality trade-offs. Highlight that internal use of POINT demonstrates composition.

slides.title: Eiffel Example: BANK_ACCOUNT

content.code:
class BANK_ACCOUNT
create make
feature {NONE} -- Initialization
    make (a_account_number: STRING)
        do
            account_number := a_account_number
            balance := 0.0
        end
feature {NONE} -- Implementation
    balance: REAL  -- Private
feature -- Access
    account_number: STRING
    get_balance: REAL
        do Result := balance end
feature -- Operations
    deposit (amount: REAL)
        require amount > 0
        do balance := balance + amount end
    withdraw (amount: REAL)
        require
            amount > 0
            amount <= balance
        do balance := balance - amount end
end

content.title: Analyze & Extend: Overdraft Protection
content.instructions: 1) Analyze: Why is balance private while account_number is public? What quality attributes does this support? 2) Apply: Sketch how to add overdraft_limit feature and modify withdraw to allow overdrafts up to the limit. Which feature clause? What precondition changes? 3) Share one design decision with a neighbor.

slides.speakerNotes: Walk through encapsulation: balance is feature {NONE} (private), enforcing information hiding. Public interface: get_balance (query), deposit/withdraw (commands). Highlight require clauses as Design by Contract preview—preconditions enforce correctness. Launch activity: students first analyze design rationale (why this encapsulation?), then apply by extending functionality. This combines analytical thinking with practical application. During debrief, emphasize that overdraft_limit should be private, withdraw precondition becomes 'amount <= balance + overdraft_limit', supporting extendibility without breaking encapsulation. Collect solutions showing different approaches to initialization and validation.

slides.title: Course Roadmap: Your Learning Path

content.prompt: Course dependency graph showing progression of topics. Foundation layer: 'Classes & Objects', 'Encapsulation'. Construction layer (arrows from foundation): 'Inheritance', 'Polymorphism', 'Genericity'. Architecture layer (arrows from construction): 'Design Patterns', 'Large-Scale Structure'. Engineering layer (arrows from all): 'Agile Methods', 'Requirements', 'Quality Processes'. Use different colors for each layer, arrows showing dependencies.

content.title: Map Your Learning: Predict & Connect
content.instructions: Study the roadmap. Choose ONE upcoming topic (inheritance, polymorphism, design patterns, or agile methods). In 3 minutes: 1) Predict: Which quality attribute(s) will this topic primarily support? Why? 2) Connect: How might this topic build on encapsulation from today? Write 2-3 sentences, then share with a neighbor.

slides.speakerNotes: Present the roadmap as a learning journey with clear dependencies. Launch activity to activate predictive thinking: students analyze how future topics connect to today's foundations and quality attributes. Common predictions: inheritance supports extendibility/reusability, polymorphism enables robustness through flexible interfaces, design patterns support reusability, agile supports correctness through iteration. During debrief, validate predictions and emphasize that each layer builds systematically—you can't master patterns without polymorphism, can't apply agile without understanding quality attributes. This metacognitive exercise helps students see the course as integrated rather than isolated topics.

slides.title: Summary and Next Steps

blocks.content: Key Takeaways

items: Software engineering requires systematic approaches
Four quality attributes: correctness, robustness, extendibility, reusability
Object-oriented programming supports quality through encapsulation
Classes are templates, objects are instances
Eiffel provides clear notation for learning OO concepts

blocks.content: Next lecture: Inheritance and Polymorphism
Action items: Install Eiffel environment, read Touch of Class chapters 1-3, complete first tutorial exercise

slides.speakerNotes: Recap the main points: (1) Software engineering is essential for industrial systems - ad-hoc approaches fail. (2) Quality attributes are the foundation - correctness, robustness, extendibility, reusability. (3) Object-oriented programming provides mechanisms to achieve quality. (4) Classes and objects are fundamental concepts, with encapsulation as key principle. (5) Eiffel notation will be our vehicle for learning. Remind students of action items: install Eiffel, read assigned chapters, attend tutorials. Preview next lecture: inheritance (extending classes) and polymorphism (flexibility through type relationships). Encourage questions and office hour visits.

slides.title: Introduction to Software Engineering and Object-Oriented Fundamentals

blocks.content: Lecture 1: Introduction to Software Engineering and Object-Oriented Fundamentals
Software Construction, Architecture and Engineering

content.title: Analyze: Your Software Engineering Experience
content.instructions: Reflect on a software project you've worked on. Identify one concrete example where the code worked correctly but was difficult to modify or reuse. What made it problematic? Write down the specific issue (tight coupling, unclear structure, hardcoded values, etc.).
content.purpose: Activate prior knowledge; diagnose gap between 'working code' and 'engineered systems'

slides.speakerNotes: Welcome students warmly. Launch the reflection activity immediately to activate prior experience and surface the central problem this course addresses: code that works isn't enough. After 2 minutes, ask 2-3 volunteers to share examples. Listen for themes like 'couldn't change X without breaking Y' or 'copy-pasted code everywhere.' Use their responses to preview that this course provides systematic principles (quality attributes, OO design) to prevent these problems. This diagnostic helps students see why engineering discipline matters beyond basic programming competence.

slides.title: Course Structure and Objectives

blocks.content: Your Learning Journey

items: Three pillars: Construction (correctness), Architecture (structure), Engineering (long-term quality)
35h lectures + 35h tutorials + 55h independent study
Assessment: 50% written exam + 50% portfolio demonstrating pillar integration
Eiffel notation → transferable OO principles for any language

content.title: Evaluate & Create: Diagnose and Redesign
content.instructions: Select a past project. (1) Evaluate it against all three pillars using a 1-5 scale for each. (2) Identify your weakest pillar. (3) Propose one concrete improvement that would strengthen that pillar (e.g., 'Add input validation for Construction' or 'Extract reusable modules for Architecture'). Share your proposal with a neighbor and explain why it addresses the gap.
content.purpose: Self-assess learning needs; create actionable improvement linked to course pillars

slides.speakerNotes: Present the three-pillar framework with brief examples: Construction ensures correctness through contracts, Architecture organizes complexity via modularity, Engineering sustains quality over decades through reusability and extendibility. Launch the activity to make pillars diagnostic and actionable. Circulate during pair discussions, listening for whether students grasp pillar distinctions. Debrief by collecting 2-3 proposed improvements and highlighting how the course provides systematic techniques for each. Emphasize that portfolio assessment rewards demonstrating growth across all pillars, not just producing working code. This activity raises cognitive demand to evaluate (self-assess against criteria) and create (propose targeted solution).

slides.title: The Software Engineering Challenge

blocks.content: Why Software Engineering Matters

items: Modern systems: millions of lines, decades of evolution
Industrial software ≠ academic exercises
Ad-hoc approaches fail at scale → systematic methods required
Example: Ariane 5 ($500M loss from reused code without analysis)

content.title: Analyze & Diagnose: From Failure to Principle
content.instructions: Read: Ariane 5 reused Ariane 4 altitude code. The new rocket's faster acceleration caused integer overflow, triggering self-destruct 37 seconds after launch. Which quality attribute(s) were violated? What engineering practice would have prevented this? Discuss with a neighbor, then propose one specific verification step the team should have performed.
content.purpose: Apply quality attributes to analyze real failure; connect abstract principles to concrete engineering practices

slides.speakerNotes: Present the Ariane 5 case as a concrete failure illustrating why systematic engineering matters. Launch the activity to move students from passively hearing the story to actively diagnosing it using quality concepts. Expected answers: robustness violated (didn't handle unexpected input range), extendibility violated (reuse without adaptation). Prevention: specification analysis, range testing, contracts. Debrief by collecting proposed verification steps, highlighting that engineering discipline means validating assumptions during reuse. This raises cognitive demand to analyze (diagnose root cause) and apply (map failure to quality framework), preparing students for the detailed quality attributes in Slide 4.

slides.title: Quality Attributes: The Foundation

blocks.content: Four Pillars of Software Quality

items: Correctness: Does it do what it should?
Robustness: Does it handle the unexpected?
Extendibility: Can it adapt to change?
Reusability: Can we leverage it elsewhere?

content.title: Diagnose, Classify & Propose Solutions
content.instructions: Online banking system scenarios: (1) Transfer moves $99 instead of $100. (2) System crashes on text in amount field. (3) Adding crypto requires rewriting transaction code. (4) Authentication can't be reused in mobile app. First, classify which quality attribute each violates. Then, propose one concrete design decision or practice that would prevent scenario (3). Share your solution with a neighbor and refine it together.
content.deliverable: Classification + one specific prevention strategy for extendibility failure

slides.speakerNotes: After introducing the four attributes, launch the activity. Give 90 seconds for individual classification and solution proposal, then 90 seconds pair discussion to refine prevention strategies, finally 60 seconds class debrief. Expected classifications: (1) correctness, (2) robustness, (3) extendibility, (4) reusability. For scenario 3, look for answers like 'use abstract payment interface' or 'separate transaction logic from payment method.' This elevates from pure classification to proposing preventive design decisions, bridging analysis to evaluation/creation. Highlight that quality attributes guide concrete architectural choices, preparing students for deeper attribute exploration in subsequent slides.

slides.title: Correctness: Doing the Right Thing

blocks.content: Correctness

items: Performs exact tasks as specified
Binary property: correct or incorrect
Requires clear, formal specifications
Most fundamental quality attribute

content.title: Identify Correctness Violations
content.instructions: Analyze this code snippet: A sort_list function specification states 'Sort integers in ascending order.' Implementation uses bubble sort but has condition: if (list[i] > list[i+1]) swap(). Which input reveals incorrectness? (A) [3,1,2] (B) [-5,3,-1] (C) [1,2,3] (D) All work correctly. Identify the answer and explain why it violates the specification.
content.deliverable: Answer selection with one-sentence justification

slides.speakerNotes: Launch activity immediately after defining correctness. Answer is D—the code is actually correct for the specification. This challenges students to analyze specification-implementation alignment rather than just spotting bugs. After polling, reveal answer and emphasize that correctness requires complete specification coverage. If time permits, modify scenario: change spec to 'Sort all numbers' but keep integer-only implementation—now inputs with floats reveal incorrectness. Connect to next slide: correctness assumes valid inputs; invalid inputs relate to robustness.

slides.title: Robustness: Handling the Unexpected

blocks.content: Robustness

items: Graceful response to abnormal conditions
Complements correctness (exceptional vs. normal cases)
Error handling and exception management
Fail-safe design: maintain safety under failure

content.title: Diagnose Robustness Failures
content.instructions: Analyze these two implementations of withdraw(amount) for a bank account: (A) Subtracts amount from balance without checks. (B) Checks if amount > balance, displays 'Error: Insufficient funds' and prevents withdrawal. For each scenario, identify which implementation fails robustness and explain what abnormal condition is mishandled: (1) User enters -50 as amount (2) Database connection drops mid-withdrawal (3) User enters 'abc' as amount. Propose one improvement for the most critical gap.
content.deliverable: Identify failure cases and propose one robustness enhancement

slides.speakerNotes: Launch activity after defining robustness. Both implementations have robustness gaps: (A) fails all scenarios; (B) handles overdraft but not negative inputs, connection failures, or type errors. Critical gap is transaction consistency (scenario 2). Students should recognize robustness requires anticipating multiple abnormal conditions beyond obvious cases. After pairs discuss, poll for most critical gap and collect improvement proposals (e.g., transaction rollback, input validation). Connect to extendibility: robust error handling structures affect how easily we add new validations later.

slides.title: Extendibility: Embracing Change

blocks.content: Extendibility

items: Ease of adapting to specification changes
Change is inevitable in software
Modular design and separation of concerns
Localized changes vs. ripple effects
Design for change from day one

content.prompt: Side-by-side comparison showing two system architectures. Left side (Good): modular boxes with one highlighted in red showing localized change, other modules unaffected. Right side (Poor): tangled web of dependencies with one change in red causing ripple effects (shown in orange) throughout system. Label: 'Well-designed vs. Poorly-designed System Response to Change'

slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize that requirements always change - new features, regulatory updates, business pivots. Example: e-commerce system adding cryptocurrency payment without restructuring entire checkout. Good design localizes changes: adding new payment method shouldn't require modifying inventory management. Mention the Open-Closed Principle preview: open for extension, closed for modification. Poor extendibility leads to maintenance nightmares and eventual system rewrites. Object-oriented mechanisms like inheritance and polymorphism support extendibility.

slides.title: Reusability: Leveraging Existing Solutions

blocks.content: Reusability

items: Using software elements across multiple applications
Economic benefits: reduced time and cost
Libraries, frameworks, and components
Trade-off: generality vs. specificity
Requires upfront design investment

content.prompt: Pyramid diagram showing reusability spectrum. Base (widest): 'Widely Reusable Libraries' (e.g., data structures, math). Middle: 'Domain-Specific Frameworks' (e.g., web, games). Top (narrowest): 'Application-Specific Code'. Arrows showing decreasing reusability upward, increasing specialization upward.

slides.speakerNotes: Highlight economic impact: reusable components dramatically reduce development time. Example: standard library collections (List, Set, Map) used in millions of applications - imagine if every project reimplemented these! Discuss the reusability spectrum: highly general (math libraries) to domain-specific (authentication modules) to application-specific. Note the paradox: making something reusable requires more effort upfront (generalization, documentation, testing) but pays dividends across projects. Object-oriented features like inheritance and generics enable reusability.

slides.title: Quality Attributes: Trade-offs in Practice

blocks.content: Analyzing Quality Attribute Trade-offs

Three systems with different priorities: (A) Medical device firmware—safety-critical, infrequent updates. (B) E-commerce platform—frequent feature additions, third-party integrations. (C) Scientific computation library—used across multiple research domains.

content.title: Evaluate & Propose (5 min)
content.instructions: For each system, rank the four quality attributes by priority AND propose one concrete design decision that reflects your ranking. Example: 'Medical device prioritizes correctness, so I'd require formal verification of all updates before deployment.' Think individually (1.5 min), discuss with neighbor (2.5 min), share one proposal (1 min).
content.deliverable: Ranking + specific design decision for at least one system

items: Medical: Correctness/Robustness > Extendibility (formal methods, extensive testing, update restrictions)
E-commerce: Extendibility > Performance (plugin architecture, API versioning, feature flags)
Library: Reusability/Correctness > Specificity (generic interfaces, comprehensive test suites)
Trade-offs require explicit design choices—not just priorities

slides.speakerNotes: This enhanced activity pushes students from evaluation to creation by requiring concrete design proposals. After pair discussions, solicit 2-3 design decisions per system and probe how they operationalize priorities. Highlight examples: medical devices might use immutable data structures (correctness), e-commerce might adopt microservices (extendibility), libraries might use abstract base classes (reusability). Emphasize that recognizing trade-offs is insufficient—engineers must translate priorities into architectural choices. Preview that OO mechanisms (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism) provide systematic tools for implementing these decisions, which upcoming slides will explore.

slides.title: Why Object-Oriented Programming?

blocks.content: Evaluating OO vs. Procedural Approaches

Scenario: Library management system tracking books, members, and loans. Two designs: (A) Procedural—separate data files (books.dat, members.dat) with functions process_loan(), calculate_fine(), update_inventory(). (B) Object-Oriented—classes BOOK, MEMBER, LOAN with encapsulated data and methods.

content.title: Design Evaluation (4 min)
content.instructions: Compare both designs against our four quality attributes. Which approach better supports correctness, robustness, extendibility, and reusability? Identify one specific advantage OO provides. Think individually (1 min), discuss with neighbor (2 min), share verdict (1 min).
content.deliverable: Justify your choice: which design would you recommend and why?

items: OO: Encapsulation protects invariants (correctness/robustness)
OO: Adding late fee policy modifies LOAN class only (extendibility)
Procedural: Changes ripple across multiple functions
OO: MEMBER class reusable in other university systems (reusability)

slides.speakerNotes: This evaluate-level activity asks students to critically assess design paradigms rather than passively accepting OO superiority. After pair discussions, poll the room and probe reasoning. Highlight that procedural design scatters related logic (loan processing touches multiple files/functions), making changes risky. OO localizes changes: adding email notifications affects MEMBER class only. Emphasize encapsulation's role: BOOK ensures valid ISBN, LOAN enforces return dates—invariants protected by design. Connect back to Slide 9's trade-offs: OO systematically supports quality attributes through structural mechanisms, not just conventions.

slides.title: Classes: Blueprints for Objects

blocks.content: Classes

items: Template defining structure and behavior
Attributes (data) and methods (operations)
Class as a type in the type system
Abstract data type with hidden implementation
Unit of modularity and reuse

content.prompt: UML class diagram showing BANK_ACCOUNT class. Top section: class name 'BANK_ACCOUNT'. Middle section (attributes): '- balance: REAL', '- account_number: STRING'. Bottom section (methods): '+ deposit(amount: REAL)', '+ withdraw(amount: REAL)', '+ get_balance(): REAL'. Use standard UML notation with minus for private, plus for public.

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce class as fundamental OO concept: a blueprint or template. Analogy: architectural blueprint defines structure of houses, class defines structure of objects. Class contains attributes (data, state) and methods (operations, behavior). Example: BANK_ACCOUNT class defines what it means to be a bank account - every account has balance and account number, supports deposit and withdraw. Class is also a type: variables can be declared of class type. Emphasize that class is abstract - it's a definition, not a concrete entity (that's an object).

slides.title: Objects: Runtime Instances

blocks.content: Objects

items: Runtime instance of a class
Each object has unique identity
Object state: current attribute values
Lifecycle: creation, use, destruction
Multiple objects from same class

content.prompt: Object diagram showing three BANK_ACCOUNT instances. Top: BANK_ACCOUNT class box. Below, three object boxes connected to class with dashed arrows: 'alice_account' (balance: 1000.0, account_number: 'A001'), 'bob_account' (balance: 2500.0, account_number: 'B002'), 'carol_account' (balance: 500.0, account_number: 'C003'). Label: 'Class and its Instances'

slides.speakerNotes: Distinguish class (abstract template) from object (concrete instance). Analogy: blueprint vs. actual houses built from it. Each object has identity (alice_account ≠ bob_account even if they have same balance), state (current values of all attributes), and behavior (responds to method calls). Objects are created at runtime, exist in memory, and eventually destroyed. Multiple objects can be created from same class, each with different state. Example: three bank accounts for Alice, Bob, Carol - all instances of BANK_ACCOUNT but with different balances and account numbers.

slides.title: Encapsulation: Information Hiding

blocks.content: Encapsulation

items: Bundling data with operations
Separating interface from implementation
Public interface vs. private details
Access control: public, private, protected
Benefits: reduced coupling, easier maintenance

content.prompt: Conceptual diagram of an object as a circle with thick boundary. Inside (private): 'balance: 1000.0', 'internal_state', 'implementation details'. Outside boundary (public interface): arrows pointing to 'deposit()', 'withdraw()', 'get_balance()'. External clients shown as small boxes outside, accessing only through public interface. Label: 'Encapsulation Boundary'

slides.speakerNotes: Encapsulation is crucial for quality: it's the mechanism that enables extendibility and reusability. Two aspects: (1) bundling data with operations that manipulate it, (2) hiding implementation details. Example: BANK_ACCOUNT balance is private - clients can't directly modify it, must use deposit/withdraw methods. This enforces invariants (balance never goes negative) and allows implementation changes (store balance in cents vs. dollars) without affecting clients. Analogy: car dashboard (public interface) vs. engine internals (private implementation). Encapsulation reduces coupling between components.

slides.title: Introduction to Eiffel

blocks.content: Eiffel: A Language for Quality Software

items: Designed specifically for software engineering principles
Strong support for Design by Contract
Clear, readable syntax emphasizing concepts over tricks
Advanced features: inheritance, genericity, multiple inheritance

content.title: Analyze: Language Choice Trade-offs
content.instructions: Consider these two scenarios: (1) Teaching software quality principles to MSc students, (2) Building a commercial web application. In pairs, analyze which language characteristics matter most for each scenario and justify whether Eiffel or a mainstream language (Java/Python) better serves each purpose. Focus on how language features support or hinder the four quality attributes.

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce Eiffel and address 'Why not Java/Python?' Answer: Eiffel was designed by Bertrand Meyer specifically to teach software engineering principles with clean syntax emphasizing concepts. Design by Contract is built-in. The activity asks students to analyze trade-offs between pedagogical clarity and industry adoption, connecting language features to quality attributes from earlier slides. This develops critical evaluation skills: recognizing that tool choice depends on context and priorities. Debrief by emphasizing concept transferability—principles learned in Eiffel apply everywhere, like learning music theory on piano helps with any instrument.

slides.title: Eiffel Class Structure

content.code:
class POINT
create make
feature {NONE} -- Initialization
    make (a_x, a_y: REAL)
        do
            x := a_x
            y := a_y
        end
feature -- Access
    x: REAL
    y: REAL
feature -- Measurement
    distance_to (other: POINT): REAL
        do
            Result := sqrt((x - other.x)^2 + (y - other.y)^2)
        end
end

content.title: Create: Design CIRCLE Class
content.instructions: Design a complete CIRCLE class with center (POINT), radius (REAL), and operations: make, area, contains (tests if a point is inside). Sketch the class structure showing: (1) Which features are public/private and why, (2) How your design supports correctness and encapsulation, (3) One precondition that prevents misuse. Share your design rationale with a neighbor, focusing on which quality attributes your decisions prioritize.

slides.speakerNotes: Walk through POINT syntax: class/create clauses, feature grouping, attributes versus methods, Result keyword, assignment operator. Emphasize feature {NONE} for private initialization. Launch activity: students synthesize a complete class design from scratch, integrating syntax patterns with quality principles from earlier slides. This elevates from applying a single pattern to creating a cohesive design. During debrief, collect designs on board showing different encapsulation choices (is radius public?), preconditions (radius > 0 in make), and how decisions reflect quality trade-offs. Highlight that internal use of POINT demonstrates composition.

slides.title: Eiffel Example: BANK_ACCOUNT

content.code:
class BANK_ACCOUNT
create make
feature {NONE} -- Initialization
    make (a_account_number: STRING)
        do
            account_number := a_account_number
            balance := 0.0
        end
feature {NONE} -- Implementation
    balance: REAL  -- Private
feature -- Access
    account_number: STRING
    get_balance: REAL
        do Result := balance end
feature -- Operations
    deposit (amount: REAL)
        require amount > 0
        do balance := balance + amount end
    withdraw (amount: REAL)
        require
            amount > 0
            amount <= balance
        do balance := balance - amount end
end

content.title: Analyze & Extend: Overdraft Protection
content.instructions: 1) Analyze: Why is balance private while account_number is public? What quality attributes does this support? 2) Apply: Sketch how to add overdraft_limit feature and modify withdraw to allow overdrafts up to the limit. Which feature clause? What precondition changes? 3) Share one design decision with a neighbor.

slides.speakerNotes: Walk through encapsulation: balance is feature {NONE} (private), enforcing information hiding. Public interface: get_balance (query), deposit/withdraw (commands). Highlight require clauses as Design by Contract preview—preconditions enforce correctness. Launch activity: students first analyze design rationale (why this encapsulation?), then apply by extending functionality. This combines analytical thinking with practical application. During debrief, emphasize that overdraft_limit should be private, withdraw precondition becomes 'amount <= balance + overdraft_limit', supporting extendibility without breaking encapsulation. Collect solutions showing different approaches to initialization and validation.

slides.title: Course Roadmap: Your Learning Path

content.prompt: Course dependency graph showing progression of topics. Foundation layer: 'Classes & Objects', 'Encapsulation'. Construction layer (arrows from foundation): 'Inheritance', 'Polymorphism', 'Genericity'. Architecture layer (arrows from construction): 'Design Patterns', 'Large-Scale Structure'. Engineering layer (arrows from all): 'Agile Methods', 'Requirements', 'Quality Processes'. Use different colors for each layer, arrows showing dependencies.

content.title: Map Your Learning: Predict & Connect
content.instructions: Study the roadmap. Choose ONE upcoming topic (inheritance, polymorphism, design patterns, or agile methods). In 3 minutes: 1) Predict: Which quality attribute(s) will this topic primarily support? Why? 2) Connect: How might this topic build on encapsulation from today? Write 2-3 sentences, then share with a neighbor.

slides.speakerNotes: Present the roadmap as a learning journey with clear dependencies. Launch activity to activate predictive thinking: students analyze how future topics connect to today's foundations and quality attributes. Common predictions: inheritance supports extendibility/reusability, polymorphism enables robustness through flexible interfaces, design patterns support reusability, agile supports correctness through iteration. During debrief, validate predictions and emphasize that each layer builds systematically—you can't master patterns without polymorphism, can't apply agile without understanding quality attributes. This metacognitive exercise helps students see the course as integrated rather than isolated topics.

Four quality attributes: correctness, robustness, extendibility, reusability
Object-oriented programming supports quality through encapsulation
Classes are templates, objects are instances
Eiffel provides clear notation for learning OO concepts

(4) Classes and objects are fundamental concepts, with encapsulation as key principle. (5) Eiffel notation will be our vehicle for learning. Remind students of action items: install Eiffel, read assigned chapters, attend tutorials. Preview next lecture: inheritance (extending classes) and polymorphism (flexibility through type relationships). Encourage questions and office hour visits.

gaps: Systematic misalignment: All six learning objectives are stated at understand level, but 100% of slides with activities operate at analyze/evaluate/create levels. This creates expectation mismatch between stated objectives and actual cognitive demands.

Missing scaffolding for create-level tasks: Slide-15 jumps directly to designing a complete class without intermediate apply-level practice. Students need guided application of Eiffel syntax patterns before synthesizing original designs.

Slides 07-08 (extendibility, reusability) lack activities: These slides remain at understand level while surrounding slides engage analyze/evaluate. This creates uneven cognitive demand distribution and missed opportunities to apply quality attribute analysis.

Objective 5 (Eiffel notation) shows three-level gap: Stated as 'recognize and understand' but assessed through class design creation. Either revise objective to 'Design classes using Eiffel notation' or add intermediate apply-level activities.

This aligns expectations with MSc-level rigor.

Add apply-level scaffolding before slide-15: Insert activity where students complete partially-written Eiffel class (fill in missing features, fix syntax errors) to practice notation application before creating original designs.

Enhance slides 07-08 with analysis activities: For extendibility, provide two architectures and ask students to predict change impact. For reusability, analyze existing library components to classify reusability level and identify design decisions enabling reuse.

Create explicit Eiffel syntax reference: Add slide between 14-15 with annotated code highlighting key notation elements (feature clauses, access control, Result, assignment). Include brief recognition quiz before design activity.

lectures.title: Inheritance, Polymorphism and Dynamic Binding

outline.title: Lecture 2: Inheritance, Polymorphism and Dynamic Binding
outline.summary: This lecture provides a comprehensive exploration of advanced object-oriented programming mechanisms essential for building flexible and reusable software architectures. Students will master single and multiple inheritance hierarchies, understand polymorphism and substitutability principles, and learn how dynamic binding enables runtime flexibility. Through practical examples in Eiffel and theoretical foundations, students will gain the skills to design extensible class hierarchies and apply these mechanisms to real-world software construction challenges.
learningObjectives: Understand and apply single inheritance to create class hierarchies that promote code reuse and logical organization
Evaluate the benefits and challenges of multiple inheritance and apply appropriate design strategies
Master polymorphism and substitutability principles to write flexible, extensible code
Explain dynamic binding mechanisms and their role in achieving late binding and runtime flexibility
Distinguish between method redefinition and overriding, applying each appropriately
Implement inheritance hierarchies in Eiffel demonstrating best practices in object-oriented design

slides.title: Lecture 2: Inheritance, Polymorphism and Dynamic Binding

blocks.content: Lecture 2: Inheritance, Polymorphism and Dynamic Binding
Building Flexible and Reusable Software Architectures

content.instruction: Quick challenge: Think of a real-world system you've built or used (e.g., e-commerce, social media, game). What entities share common behavior? Sketch 2-3 classes in a hierarchy showing 'is-a' relationships.

blocks.content: Today you'll design hierarchies, evaluate inheritance strategies, and implement polymorphic solutions in Eiffel.

slides.speakerNotes: Welcome to Lecture 2. Before diving in, activate prior knowledge with the 90-second challenge. This primes students to think about inheritance as a design tool, not just a language feature. After time expires, ask 2-3 volunteers to share examples (e.g., User→Customer/Admin, Vehicle→Car/Truck). Acknowledge responses briefly without critique. Set expectations: today moves beyond understanding concepts to applying them in design scenarios and evaluating trade-offs. This opening shifts from passive introduction to active engagement, targeting apply-level thinking from the start.

slides.title: Why Inheritance Matters: Design Challenge

blocks.content: **Scenario:** You're building a university management system. You need classes for Student, Faculty, and TeachingAssistant. All share name, ID, email. Students have GPA and enroll in courses. Faculty teach courses and have research areas. TAs both take and teach courses.

content.instruction: Sketch an inheritance hierarchy for this system (2 minutes). Consider: What's the parent class? Which attributes/methods belong where? How does TA fit—single or multiple inheritance?

items: Code reuse: Shared attributes in parent class
Models 'is-a' relationships naturally
Enables polymorphism: treat all as Person
Foundation for extensible systems

slides.speakerNotes: Present the scenario and give students 2 minutes to sketch individually. Then pair-share for 1-2 minutes. Poll for solutions: Who used single inheritance with Person parent? Who needed multiple inheritance for TA? Discuss trade-offs. This applies inheritance concepts to a realistic problem, addressing the 'apply single inheritance' objective. Reveal that TA motivates multiple inheritance (covered in slides 6-9). Emphasize that inheritance models real relationships, not just code sharing.

slides.title: Inheritance in Action: Design Exercise

content.prompt: UML class diagram showing Vehicle as parent class at top with attributes (speed: INTEGER, fuel: REAL) and methods (start, stop, refuel). Three child classes below: Car, Truck, Motorcycle, each inheriting from Vehicle with specialized attributes. Use arrows pointing upward from children to parent. Clean, educational style.

content.instruction: Given this Vehicle hierarchy, sketch how you would add: (1) ElectricCar (no fuel, has batteryLevel), (2) Bicycle (no fuel/engine). Where do they fit? What attributes move or change? Does the parent class need refactoring?

items: Does ElectricCar inherit fuel attribute? (LSP issue)
Does Bicycle IS-A Vehicle if it has no engine?
Should Vehicle be more abstract?
When to use inheritance vs. composition?

slides.speakerNotes: Show the diagram, then present the challenge. Give students 2 minutes to sketch solutions individually. Poll responses: Who added ElectricCar as direct Vehicle child? Who refactored Vehicle to be more abstract (e.g., removing fuel)? Highlight that this exposes real design tensions—ElectricCar inheriting unused fuel violates LSP. Bicycle challenges the 'is-a' test. This applies inheritance design skills and previews LSP (slide 11). Emphasize that good hierarchies require thinking about future extensions, not just current needs.

slides.title: Single Inheritance: Apply the Principles

items: One parent class → tree structure
'Is-a' relationship must hold
Children inherit all features (visibility rules apply)
Foundation: Liskov Substitution Principle

content.instruction: Evaluate these proposed hierarchies. Which violates single inheritance principles? Why? (A) Employee → Manager → Director, (B) Shape → Square → Rectangle, (C) Animal → Dog → Puppy. Identify the problematic design and explain how to fix it using 'is-a' and LSP.

items: Does the child truly 'is-a' parent in all contexts?
Can child substitute for parent without breaking behavior?
Are inherited attributes meaningful for the child?

slides.speakerNotes: Present the three hierarchies. Give 90 seconds individual thinking, then 90 seconds pair discussion. Poll for answers—hierarchy B (Square→Rectangle) violates LSP because Square constrains Rectangle's behavior (width must equal height). The 'is-a' test fails: a Square cannot substitute for Rectangle in all contexts. Correct approach: make both inherit from Shape. This activity directly applies the principles just introduced and prepares students for the Vehicle design challenge on slide 3. Emphasize that recognizing violations is the first step toward creating correct hierarchies.

slides.title: Single Inheritance in Eiffel: Apply It

content.code:
class ACCOUNT
feature
    balance: REAL
    deposit (amount: REAL)
        require amount > 0
        do
            balance := balance + amount
        end
end

class SAVINGS_ACCOUNT
inherit
    ACCOUNT
feature
    interest_rate: REAL
    apply_interest
        do
            deposit(balance * interest_rate)
        end
end

content.instruction: Using the ACCOUNT hierarchy as reference, implement a CHECKING_ACCOUNT class that: (1) inherits from ACCOUNT, (2) adds a monthly_fee attribute, (3) implements deduct_fee that reduces balance by monthly_fee. Write the Eiffel code structure (class header, inherit clause, features). What precondition should deduct_fee have?

items: Which features does CHECKING_ACCOUNT inherit?
Should deduct_fee call deposit with negative amount?
What contract (require/ensure) protects balance integrity?

slides.speakerNotes: Give 2 minutes for students to sketch CHECKING_ACCOUNT code on paper or laptops. Then discuss solutions. Key points: inherits balance and deposit; deduct_fee needs 'require balance >= monthly_fee' to prevent negative balance; should NOT use deposit (violates its precondition). This directly applies Eiffel inheritance syntax and contracts, moving from observation to implementation. Connects to LSP discussion on next slides—proper preconditions ensure substitutability. Addresses the 'implement inheritance hierarchies in Eiffel' objective at apply level.

slides.title: Multiple Inheritance: Power and Complexity

items: Inherit from multiple parent classes
Combine orthogonal features (mixins)
Creates DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) structures
Supported: C++, Eiffel, Python
Not supported: Java, C# (use interfaces instead)

slides.speakerNotes: Multiple inheritance is powerful but complex. It allows combining features from multiple sources—useful for mixins or when an object genuinely has multiple roles. Emphasize the structural difference: no longer a tree, but a DAG. Many languages avoid it due to complexity; Java/C# use single inheritance + interfaces as a compromise.

slides.title: The Diamond Problem: Analysis Challenge

content.prompt: Diamond inheritance diagram showing Person class at top with 'id' attribute, Student and Employee classes in middle both inheriting from Person, and TeachingAssistant class at bottom inheriting from both Student and Employee. Highlight the conflict: which 'id' does TeachingAssistant inherit? Use red highlight or question mark to show ambiguity. Clean UML style.

content.title: Analyze & Propose
content.instructions: Given this TeachingAssistant scenario: (1) Identify all ambiguities that arise (attributes, methods, initialization). (2) Propose TWO different resolution strategies and explain trade-offs of each. (3) Which would you choose and why?

slides.speakerNotes: Present the diamond problem, then engage students in analysis. They should identify: attribute conflicts (id), potential method conflicts (display_info), and initialization issues. Expected strategies: rename both ids, select one id, use composition instead. After pair discussion, poll the room for preferences and discuss trade-offs: clarity vs. simplicity, memory duplication vs. shared state. This prepares them for Eiffel's explicit resolution approach in the next slide and addresses the evaluate objective for multiple inheritance design strategies.

slides.title: Resolving the Diamond: Eiffel Approach

content.code:
class TEACHING_ASSISTANT
inherit
    STUDENT
        rename
            id as student_id
        end
    EMPLOYEE
        rename
            id as employee_id
        end
feature
    student_id: STRING
    employee_id: STRING
    
    -- Now both IDs are accessible
    -- No ambiguity
end

slides.speakerNotes: Eiffel's solution: explicit renaming. The programmer must decide how to handle conflicts. Here we rename both 'id' attributes to make them distinct. Alternative: use 'select' to choose one. This makes the programmer's intent clear and prevents silent errors. Discuss trade-off: more verbose but safer.

slides.title: Evaluating Multiple Inheritance Design Decisions

blocks.content:
**Design Challenge:** You're building a university system. A TeachingAssistant needs properties from both Student (courses, GPA) and Employee (salary, department). Consider two approaches:

**A)** Multiple inheritance: `class TA inherit STUDENT; EMPLOYEE`

**B)** Composition: `class TA inherit STUDENT` with `employment_info: EMPLOYEE_RECORD`

content.title: Think-Pair-Share (3 min)
content.instructions:
1. Individually: Which design would you choose? List 2 pros and 2 cons for your choice (1 min)
2. Pair: Compare reasoning with a neighbor (1 min)
3. Share: Vote and justify (1 min)
content.deliverable: Be ready to defend your choice based on: code reuse, maintainability, diamond problem risk, and semantic clarity

items: Is-a vs. has-a: Does TA fundamentally *be* both roles?
Diamond risk: Could STUDENT and EMPLOYEE share ancestors?
Interface vs. implementation: Need behaviors or just data?
Language support: Does your language handle MI conflicts well?

slides.speakerNotes: This activity targets the 'evaluate benefits and challenges of MI' objective. After voting, reveal that both can work but composition often wins for orthogonal concerns like employment. MI better when TA must substitute for both Student AND Employee polymorphically. Highlight that design choice depends on substitutability needs and language features. Connect back to slide 8's renaming solution if MI chosen. Emphasize no single right answer—justification matters.

slides.title: Polymorphism: One Interface, Many Forms

items: Single interface, multiple implementations
Subtype polymorphism (inheritance-based)
Write code that works with any subtype
Enables extensibility without modification

content.prompt: Memory diagram showing an array labeled 'shapes: ARRAY[SHAPE]' containing references pointing to different objects: a Circle object, a Rectangle object, and a Triangle object. Show the array holding references (arrows) to these different concrete types. Label static type as SHAPE and dynamic types as Circle, Rectangle, Triangle.

slides.speakerNotes: Polymorphism is the ability to treat objects of different types uniformly through a common interface. The array has static type ARRAY[SHAPE], but contains objects of dynamic types Circle, Rectangle, Triangle. This is the power of polymorphism: write code once (iterate over shapes), works with any shape type, including types not yet invented.

slides.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

blocks.content: Objects of a subtype should be substitutable for objects of the supertype without altering program correctness.

items: Behavioral subtyping, not just structural
Preserve invariants and contracts
Weaken preconditions, strengthen postconditions
Violations lead to subtle bugs

slides.speakerNotes: LSP is crucial for correct inheritance. It's not enough that a Square IS-A Rectangle structurally—it must behave correctly in all contexts where Rectangle is used. Classic violation: if Rectangle has setWidth/setHeight that work independently, but Square must keep width=height, substituting Square breaks code expecting Rectangle behavior. Always think: can I use the child wherever the parent is expected?

slides.title: Polymorphism in Eiffel

content.code:
class ZOO
feature
    animals: LINKED_LIST[ANIMAL]
    
    feed_all
        local
            animal: ANIMAL
        do
            from animals.start
            until animals.after
            loop
                animal := animals.item
                animal.eat  -- Polymorphic call
                animals.forth
            end
        end
end

-- Works with Dog, Cat, Bird, etc.
-- Each implements 'eat' differently

slides.speakerNotes: This demonstrates polymorphic programming. The feed_all method works with any ANIMAL subtype. The call to animal.eat is polymorphic—which implementation runs depends on the dynamic type (Dog.eat, Cat.eat, etc.). Note that static type is ANIMAL, but dynamic type varies. This is resolved at runtime through dynamic binding, our next topic.

slides.title: Dynamic Binding: Runtime Method Resolution

items: Static binding: resolved at compile time
Dynamic binding: resolved at runtime
Enables polymorphism to work
Uses virtual method table (vtable)
Trade-off: flexibility vs. performance

slides.speakerNotes: Dynamic binding is the mechanism that makes polymorphism work. When you call animal.eat, the compiler doesn't know which eat method to call—it depends on the runtime type. Dynamic binding defers this decision to runtime using a vtable. This adds a small performance cost (indirection) but gives enormous flexibility. In Eiffel, all calls are dynamically bound by default.

slides.title: Virtual Method Table (vtable)

content.prompt: Detailed memory layout diagram showing: 1) A Dog object in memory with a vtable pointer at the top, followed by data fields. 2) The vtable pointer (arrow) pointing to Dog's vtable. 3) Dog's vtable as a table with entries: eat -> Dog.eat, sleep -> Dog.sleep, speak -> Dog.speak. 4) Show similar structure for Cat object pointing to Cat's vtable. Label clearly: 'vtable pointer', 'Dog vtable', 'method addresses'.

items: Each object has vtable pointer
Vtable maps method names to addresses
Runtime: follow pointer, lookup method, call
One vtable per class, shared by all instances

slides.speakerNotes: This is how dynamic binding works under the hood. Each object has a hidden pointer to its class's vtable. When you call animal.eat: (1) follow the vtable pointer, (2) look up 'eat' in the table, (3) call the address found. This is fast (two indirections) but slower than static calls. One vtable per class, not per object, so memory overhead is minimal.

slides.title: Method Redefinition: Apply It

content.code:
class SHAPE
feature
    area: REAL
        deferred
        end
end

class CIRCLE
inherit
    SHAPE
        redefine area end
feature
    radius: REAL
    area: REAL
        do
            Result := 3.14159 * radius * radius
        end
end

content.instruction: Design RECTANGLE and TRIANGLE classes inheriting from SHAPE. What features do they need? Implement their area methods. Would you add any deferred features to SHAPE? Discuss with a partner.
content.deliverable: Sketch class structure with features and area calculations

slides.speakerNotes: Students now apply redefinition to new shapes. Walk through CIRCLE first: deferred means no implementation in parent; redefine clause signals override; effective implementation required. Then give 3 minutes for the activity. Circulate and check designs. Common solution: RECTANGLE needs width, height; area = width * height. TRIANGLE needs base, height; area = 0.5 * base * height. Some may suggest adding perimeter as deferred. Debrief 2-3 solutions, emphasizing the redefine clause and that each subclass provides appropriate calculations.

slides.title: Using Precursor: Extending Parent Behavior

content.code:
class EMPLOYEE
feature
    calculate_salary: REAL
        do
            Result := base_salary
        end
end

class MANAGER
inherit
    EMPLOYEE
        redefine calculate_salary end
feature
    calculate_salary: REAL
        do
            Result := Precursor + bonus
            -- Calls EMPLOYEE.calculate_salary
            -- then adds bonus
        end
end

slides.speakerNotes: Precursor calls the parent's implementation. This is crucial for extending rather than replacing behavior. MANAGER.calculate_salary builds on EMPLOYEE.calculate_salary by adding a bonus. This promotes code reuse and maintains the parent's logic. Without Precursor, you'd have to duplicate the base_salary calculation. Similar to 'super' in Java or Python.

slides.title: Design Patterns: Template Method

content.prompt: UML class diagram showing Template Method pattern. Abstract class DataProcessor at top with template method 'process()' that calls abstract methods 'read_data()', 'process_data()', 'write_data()'. Two concrete classes below: CSVProcessor and JSONProcessor, each implementing the three abstract methods. Show the sequence: process() calls the three steps in order.

items: Define algorithm skeleton in parent
Subclasses customize specific steps
Parent controls overall flow
Promotes consistency and reuse

slides.speakerNotes: Template Method is a classic pattern leveraging inheritance and redefinition. The parent defines the algorithm structure (process = read, then process, then write), but leaves specific steps abstract. Each subclass provides concrete implementations. This ensures all processors follow the same flow while allowing customization. Common in frameworks. Note how this relies on dynamic binding to call the right implementations.

slides.title: Common Pitfalls and Best Practices

items: Avoid deep hierarchies (> 4-5 levels)
Favor composition over inheritance for 'has-a'
Don't break encapsulation with protected members
Ensure LSP compliance—test substitutability
Document redefinable methods clearly

slides.speakerNotes: Common mistakes: deep hierarchies become hard to understand (yo-yo problem). Use composition when objects have parts, not when they are subtypes. Protected members can break encapsulation—prefer private with protected accessors. Always test that subclasses can substitute for parents. These practices prevent the 'fragile base class' problem where changes to parents break children.

slides.title: Summary: Key Takeaways

items: Inheritance: Code reuse and modeling 'is-a' relationships
Multiple inheritance: Powerful but requires careful design
Polymorphism + LSP: Write flexible, substitutable code
Dynamic binding: Runtime method resolution via vtables
Redefinition: Customize behavior while maintaining contracts
Apply thoughtfully: Balance flexibility with complexity

slides.speakerNotes: Recap the key concepts. Inheritance is a powerful tool for reuse and modeling, but must be used thoughtfully. Polymorphism and LSP ensure correct, flexible designs. Dynamic binding is the mechanism enabling polymorphism. These concepts work together to create extendible, maintainable systems. Next lecture: genericity and parametric polymorphism. Encourage students to practice with the exercises and come to tutorial with questions.

slides.title: Looking Ahead

blocks.content: Next Topics

items: Genericity and parametric polymorphism
Design by Contract: Strengthening inheritance with contracts
Advanced design patterns using these mechanisms
Real-world case studies and applications

blocks.content: Practice: Implement the exercise hierarchies in Eiffel. Prepare questions for tutorial.

slides.speakerNotes: Preview upcoming topics to show how today's concepts fit into the bigger picture. Genericity will add another dimension of flexibility. Design by Contract will show how to make inheritance hierarchies more robust. Emphasize the importance of hands-on practice—implement the suggested exercises. Remind students of tutorial times and encourage them to bring specific questions about challenging concepts.
