Propose one improvement addressing a weakness you identified.

slides.speakerNotes: Genericity eliminates duplication through parameterized types. Before seeing syntax, design your own generic class and evaluate trade-offs. This isn't just about applying a pattern—you must create a design, then critically assess its strengths and limitations. The one-versus-two parameter decision has real consequences: flexibility versus simplicity, expressiveness versus cognitive load. After designing, step back and critique your own work. What use cases break your design? This metacognitive evaluation mirrors real-world architectural decision-making where you must justify choices and identify improvement opportunities.

slides.title: Declaring Generic Classes

items: Syntax: class ClassName[TypeParameter]
Type parameters in square brackets
Use throughout: fields, parameters, return types
Convention: G, T, E or descriptive names

content.code:
class STACK[G]
feature
  items: ARRAY[G]
  
  push (item: G)
  do
    -- implementation
  end
  
  pop: G
  do
    -- implementation
  end
end

content.title: Design from Requirements
content.instructions: You're building a library for event scheduling. Requirements: store events of any type, retrieve by priority, support filtering by criteria. Design a complete generic class architecture from scratch: choose class names, declare all type parameters with constraints if needed, sketch key method signatures, and decide what fields are required. Justify: Why did you choose your type parameter structure? What constraints (if any) did you add and why? How does your design support the filtering requirement?

slides.speakerNotes: This create-level task requires synthesizing a complete generic architecture from requirements rather than filling in a template. Students must make foundational decisions: single generic parameter or multiple? What constraints enable priority and filtering? Should filtering be a method parameter or a separate type? These choices have cascading implications. During pair discussion, compare different valid architectures and identify trade-offs. This mirrors real design work where requirements don't dictate a single solution—you must create, justify, and defend architectural choices.

slides.title: Type Instantiation

items: Provide actual type arguments when creating instances
Type inference reduces verbosity
Compile-time type safety guaranteed
Each instantiation is a distinct type

content.code:
-- Explicit type instantiation
int_stack: STACK[INTEGER]
create int_stack.make

string_stack: STACK[STRING]
create string_stack.make

-- These are distinct types
int_stack.push(42)        -- OK
string_stack.push("hello") -- OK
int_stack.push("error")   -- Compile error!

slides.speakerNotes: When creating instances, we specify the actual type. STACK[INTEGER] and STACK[STRING] are distinct types—the compiler won't let you mix them up. This is type safety in action: errors caught at compile time, not runtime.

slides.title: Constraint Design Challenge

items: Generic classes need constraints to enable operations
Too restrictive → limits reusability
Too permissive → can't implement required behavior
Design challenge: find minimal necessary constraints

content.title: Design Exercise: Determine Minimal Constraints
content.description: For each generic class below, determine the minimal type constraint needed. Justify why your constraint is both necessary and sufficient.
tasks: PRIORITY_QUEUE[G] — needs to order elements by priority
HASH_TABLE[K, V] — needs to compute hash codes for keys
SORTED_LIST[G] — needs to maintain sorted order and find duplicates

content.code:
class SORTED_LIST[G]  -- What constraint?
  insert (item: G)
  do
    if item > current_item then  -- Needs what?
      -- requires comparison
    end
  end
  
  has_duplicate (item: G): BOOLEAN
  do
    -- requires equality check
  end
end

slides.speakerNotes: This activity moves students from understanding why constraints exist to applying design judgment. They must analyze what operations each class requires, then determine the minimal interface needed—avoiding over-constraining while ensuring necessary capabilities. The SORTED_LIST example requires both comparison and equality, pushing students to think about multiple operation requirements. Discuss trade-offs: COMPARABLE vs HASHABLE vs custom interfaces. This applies constraint design to novel scenarios, building toward the create-level objective of designing generic classes.

slides.title: Implementing Type Constraints

items: Syntax: class NAME[G -> CONSTRAINT]
Type arguments must satisfy constraints
Enables calling methods from constraint type
Compiler enforces constraint satisfaction

content.code:
class SORTED_LIST[G -> COMPARABLE]
  insert (item: G)
  do
    if item > current_item then  -- Valid!
      -- comparison enabled by constraint
    end
  end
  
  find_max: G
  do
    -- Can safely compare elements
  end
end

content.title: Analyze: Constraint Necessity
content.description: For the SORTED_LIST above, evaluate what breaks if we remove the constraint. Then analyze: could we use a weaker constraint like ANY? What operations would fail? What's the minimal interface G needs to support both insert and find_max? Justify your reasoning.

slides.speakerNotes: This activity pushes students to analyze constraint necessity rather than just accepting syntax. By asking what breaks without constraints, they must trace through operations and identify dependencies. The question about weaker constraints (ANY vs COMPARABLE) requires analyzing trade-offs between flexibility and functionality. This moves from understanding syntax to analyzing why constraints exist and evaluating minimal requirements—supporting the objective of designing appropriate constraints.

slides.title: Designing with Constraints

items: Choose minimal necessary constraints
Overly restrictive = limited reusability
Design interfaces for use as constraints
Balance flexibility vs. functionality

blocks.content:
**Scenario:** Design a generic PRIORITY_QUEUE[G] that orders elements by priority. Two approaches proposed:

**A:** Constraint G -> COMPARABLE (elements self-compare)
**B:** Add separate PRIORITY_FUNCTION parameter, no constraint on G

content.title: Evaluate: Constraint Trade-offs
content.explanation: Compare approaches A and B. For each: (1) What use cases does it support well? (2) What use cases does it prevent? (3) Which is more reusable and why? Then propose a third approach that combines strengths of both. Justify which approach you'd choose for a general-purpose library.

slides.speakerNotes: This evaluation task requires students to analyze trade-offs between constraint designs rather than just applying rules. Approach A is simpler but forces G to be comparable. Approach B is more flexible but more complex. Strong answers recognize that approach B enables priority queues over non-comparable types (like tasks prioritized by external rules). The best solution might combine both: allow optional priority function with COMPARABLE as fallback. This develops judgment in constraint design—a key skill for creating reusable components.

slides.title: Information Hiding: Design Challenge

blocks.content: "Modules should hide design decisions that are likely to change from other modules." —David Parnas

items: Scenario: STUDENT_REGISTRY class manages enrollment
Current: public array 'students', public 'count' field
Clients directly access: registry.students[i], registry.count
Problem: Need to switch from array to hash table

content.title: Apply Information Hiding
content.explanation: Redesign STUDENT_REGISTRY to hide the storage implementation. Determine: (1) Which members should be private vs public? (2) What public methods should replace direct access? (3) How does your design allow switching from array to hash table without breaking client code? Justify each visibility decision.

slides.speakerNotes: This activity requires applying information hiding to solve a realistic problem. Students must analyze what should be hidden, design a proper interface, and justify their decisions. The scenario mirrors real evolution challenges. After individual work, discuss solutions: make storage and count private, provide methods like enroll(), find(), remove(). This demonstrates how hiding implementation details enables changing data structures without affecting clients—the core value of information hiding.

slides.title: Applying Information Hiding: Design Analysis

items: Given: EMPLOYEE_DATABASE class with public fields 'employees: ARRAY[EMPLOYEE]' and 'size: INTEGER'
Clients use: db.employees[i].salary := 50000
New requirement: Add audit logging for all salary changes
Challenge: Current design makes this impossible without changing all client code

content.title: Redesign for Information Hiding
content.explanation: Redesign EMPLOYEE_DATABASE applying information hiding. (1) Identify what to hide and what to expose. (2) Design public methods to replace direct access. (3) Explain how your design enables audit logging without breaking clients. (4) Analyze trade-offs: what flexibility does hiding provide vs. what convenience does direct access lose?

slides.speakerNotes: This shifts from passive explanation to active application and analysis. Students must apply information hiding principles to solve a realistic problem, then analyze trade-offs. After individual work, discuss solutions: hide employees array and size, expose update_salary(), get_employee() methods. The key insight: hiding implementation creates an interception point for cross-cutting concerns like logging. Discuss the trade-off: clients lose direct access convenience but gain flexibility for system evolution. This demonstrates why information hiding is worth the initial design effort.

slides.title: Access Control Levels: Design Decisions

content.code:
class STUDENT_REGISTRY
  students: ARRAY[STUDENT]
  enrollment_count: INTEGER
  max_capacity: INTEGER
  
  enroll(s: STUDENT)
  drop(s: STUDENT)
  find_by_id(id: STRING): STUDENT
  validate_enrollment(s: STUDENT): BOOLEAN
  update_statistics
  get_enrollment_count: INTEGER
end

content.title: Apply Access Control
content.explanation: For each feature in STUDENT_REGISTRY, decide: private, protected, or public? Justify each choice considering: (1) what clients need vs implementation details, (2) future flexibility for changes, (3) preventing misuse. Then identify one consequence of making 'students' public vs private.

slides.speakerNotes: Students must apply access control principles to make design decisions, not just recall definitions. Expected: students array and update_statistics private (implementation details), validate_enrollment private or protected (helper), public interface minimal (enroll, drop, find_by_id, get_enrollment_count). Key insight: exposing 'students' directly allows clients to bypass enroll/drop logic, breaking invariants. After individual work, compare decisions and discuss trade-offs. This bridges to slide 13's BANK_ACCOUNT example showing proper separation.

slides.title: Designing Class Interfaces

content.code:
class BANK_ACCOUNT
feature -- Access
  balance: DECIMAL
  deposit (amount: DECIMAL)
  withdraw (amount: DECIMAL)

feature {NONE} -- Implementation
  transaction_log: LINKED_LIST[TRANSACTION]
  validate_amount (amount: DECIMAL): BOOLEAN
  update_audit_trail
end

-- What if balance were feature {NONE}?
-- What if transaction_log were public?
-- What if validate_amount were public?

content.title: Design Interface & Justify Decisions
content.explanation: Design the public interface for class EMAIL_QUEUE with features: messages (array), add_message, send_next, retry_failed, last_error, validate_recipient, log_activity, message_count. For each feature, decide public or private and write one-sentence justification. Then: identify two problems that occur if 'messages' is public instead of private.

slides.speakerNotes: Students must apply interface design principles to make and justify access control decisions. Expected reasoning: messages private (prevent bypassing queue logic), add_message/send_next/message_count public (core operations), validate_recipient/log_activity/retry_failed private (implementation details). Key insight: exposing messages allows clients to manipulate queue directly, breaking ordering guarantees and bypassing validation. After individual work, compare decisions in pairs. This builds on slide 12's activity and prepares for slide 14's contract discussion.

slides.title: Interface as Contract

items: Interface defines WHAT, not HOW
Specifies signatures, preconditions, postconditions
Forms contract between provider and client
Stable interface, evolving implementation

content.title: Analyze Interface Separation Quality
content.explanation: Three designs for interface CACHE<K,V> are provided. Design A: get(key), put(key,value), size(). Design B: get(key), put(key,value), getInternalArray(), rehash(), size(). Design C: get(key), put(key,value), clear(), contains(key). Analyze each: (1) Identify which exposes implementation details (leaky abstraction). (2) Rank designs from best to worst separation. (3) Justify ranking with specific problems in weaker designs. (4) Propose one improvement to Design C.

slides.speakerNotes: Students analyze interface designs to distinguish good separation from leaky abstractions. Design B clearly violates separation by exposing getInternalArray() and rehash(). Expected ranking: C > A > B. Key insight: B locks clients into array-based implementation and breaks encapsulation. Design C is strongest but could add remove(key) for completeness. This analyze-level task directly addresses the objective 'distinguish between interface and implementation' and prepares students for slide 15's programming-to-interfaces principle. Discuss findings in pairs before class debrief.

slides.title: Programming to Interfaces

items: Depend on abstractions, not concrete classes
Enables substitutability and flexibility
Facilitates testing with mock implementations
Supports plugin architectures

content.title: Refactor to Interface Dependencies
content.explanation: Given code: class ReportGenerator { private MySQLDatabase db = new MySQLDatabase(); void generate() { db.connect(); List<Record> data = db.query("SELECT..."); /*process*/ } }. Tasks: (1) Identify all concrete dependencies that limit flexibility. (2) Refactor to use interface types, introducing a Database interface. (3) Explain how your refactoring enables: testing with mock databases, switching to PostgreSQL, supporting multiple database backends simultaneously. (4) Identify injection points for dependency injection.

slides.speakerNotes: Students apply programming-to-interfaces by refactoring concrete dependencies. Expected solution introduces Database interface, changes field type to Database, uses constructor injection. This apply-level task directly addresses 'distinguish between interface and implementation' by requiring students to identify separation boundaries and demonstrate flexibility gains. Key insight: concrete class in field declaration locks implementation; interface enables runtime substitution. Discuss testing and plugin scenarios. Prepares for slide 16's synthesis of genericity and information hiding.

slides.title: Combining Genericity and Information Hiding

items: Generic interfaces with hidden implementations
Type flexibility + implementation concealment
Single generic interface, multiple implementations
Change internals without affecting type-safe clients

content.title: Design a Generic Cache System
content.explanation: Design CACHE<K,V> from requirements: (1) Create interface with put, get, remove, size operations. (2) Design two implementations: LRU_CACHE (evicts least-recently-used) and TTL_CACHE (time-to-live expiration). (3) Specify type constraints on K and V with justification. (4) Identify what implementation details to hide and what to expose in interface. (5) Explain how clients benefit from both genericity and information hiding.

slides.speakerNotes: Students now create a complete generic component integrating both principles. This create-level task addresses multiple objectives: designing generic classes with constraints, building reusable components, and establishing clean interface-implementation boundaries. Expected solution: CACHE<K,V> interface with operations; LRU_CACHE uses linked structure (hidden); TTL_CACHE uses timestamps (hidden); K constrained to HASHABLE; eviction policies completely encapsulated. Discussion should highlight how interface stability enables swapping implementations and how genericity enables reuse across types. This prepares students for the collection framework case study in slide 17.

slides.title: Case Study: Collection Frameworks

items: Generic type parameters for elements
Interface hierarchy hides implementation diversity
Constrained genericity for specialized collections
Information hiding in data structure choices

content.prompt: Simplified UML class diagram of collection framework. Top: Collection<E> interface. Below: List<E>, Set<E>, Map<K,V> interfaces. Bottom level: ArrayList<E>, LinkedList<E> implementing List; HashSet<E>, TreeSet<E> implementing Set; HashMap<K,V>, TreeMap<K,V> implementing Map. Use different colors for interfaces vs implementations.

slides.speakerNotes: Real-world example: Java Collections Framework. Generic interfaces at top—Collection<E>, List<E>, Set<E>. Multiple implementations below—ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, TreeSet. Clients program to interfaces, get type safety through generics, and remain independent of implementation choices. This is professional library design.

slides.title: Key Takeaways

items: Genericity enables type-safe reuse across types
Constraints balance flexibility with required functionality
Information hiding manages complexity through encapsulation
Interface-implementation separation enables evolution
Together: robust, reusable, maintainable components

content.prompt: Concept map showing central node 'Reusable Software Components' with four connected nodes: 'Genericity' (type parameters, constraints), 'Information Hiding' (private implementation), 'Interface Separation' (contract vs implementation), and 'Quality Attributes' (maintainability, extensibility, correctness). Use arrows to show relationships and contributions.

slides.speakerNotes: Let's synthesize: Genericity gives us type-safe reuse. Information hiding manages complexity. Interface separation enables evolution. Together, these principles let us build components that are reusable across contexts, maintainable over time, and correct by construction. These aren't just academic concepts—they're the foundation of professional software engineering. Master them, and you'll write better code for your entire career.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Understand and apply generic programming concepts to create reusable software components
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 4-6 require students to design generic classes from scratch (PAIR container, event scheduling system), moving beyond understanding syntax to applying genericity principles in novel contexts. Activities demand creating complete architectures with justified design decisions.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Design and implement generic classes with appropriate type parameters and constraints
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 5, 7, 9, and 16 explicitly require designing generic classes from requirements. Slide 5 asks students to design event scheduling architecture with type parameters and constraints. Slide 7 requires determining minimal necessary constraints. Slide 16 synthesizes both principles in cache system design. These are create-level tasks requiring original architectural decisions.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Apply information hiding principles to manage complexity in large-scale systems
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 10-11 present realistic scenarios (STUDENT_REGISTRY, EMPLOYEE_DATABASE) requiring students to apply information hiding to solve evolution problems. Students must redesign classes to hide implementation details and enable changes like switching data structures or adding audit logging without breaking clients.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Implement proper access control and visibility mechanisms for encapsulation
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 12-13 require applying access control decisions to realistic classes (STUDENT_REGISTRY, EMAIL_QUEUE, BANK_ACCOUNT). Students must decide public vs private for each feature and justify decisions based on client needs, future flexibility, and preventing misuse. These are application tasks with justification requirements.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Distinguish between interface and implementation, designing clean separation boundaries
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slide 14 requires analyzing three CACHE interface designs to identify leaky abstractions and rank separation quality. Slide 15 requires identifying concrete dependencies and refactoring to interface types. Both tasks require breaking down designs to distinguish interface from implementation concerns and assessing separation quality.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Build reusable library components following best practices in object-oriented design
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slide 16's cache system design synthesizes all principles, requiring students to create a complete generic component with interface-implementation separation, appropriate constraints, and hidden implementation details. This directly addresses building reusable components. Slide 5's event scheduling design also requires creating library-quality architectures from requirements.

lectures.title: Design by Contract: Assertions and Program Correctness

outline.title: Lecture 4. Design by Contract: Assertions and Program Correctness
outline.summary: This lecture introduces Design by Contract (DbC) methodology as a systematic approach to building reliable software. Students will learn to specify software behavior using preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants, understand how contracts guarantee program correctness, and apply assertion-based reasoning to ensure software quality. The lecture emphasizes practical application of DbC principles in object-oriented programming and their role in achieving program reliability.
learningObjectives: Understand the fundamental principles and philosophy of Design by Contract
Write and apply preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants to specify software behavior
Use assertions for runtime monitoring and debugging
Apply contract inheritance rules and understand behavioral subtyping
Evaluate how contracts contribute to program reliability and correctness
Integrate DbC techniques into object-oriented software construction practices

sections.title: Introduction to Design by Contract
learningGoals: Understand the motivation for formal contracts in software
Grasp the philosophical foundation of DbC
Recognize the relationship between contracts and program correctness

subsections.title: The Software Reliability Challenge
keyPoints: Software defects cost billions annually and can cause catastrophic failures
Traditional testing catches errors but cannot prove correctness
Need for systematic methods to specify and verify software behavior
DbC provides a bridge between informal specifications and formal verification
examples: Ariane 5 rocket failure due to contract violation (overflow)
Medical device failures from unspecified preconditions
Financial system errors from missing postconditions
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Timeline showing evolution from ad-hoc testing to formal methods, highlighting DbC's position

subsections.title: The Contract Metaphor
keyPoints: Contracts as agreements between software components (client and supplier)
Each party has obligations and benefits
Client obligation: satisfy precondition; Benefit: postcondition guaranteed
Supplier obligation: establish postcondition; Benefit: assume precondition
Contracts make implicit assumptions explicit and verifiable
examples: Real-world contract: hiring a contractor to build a house
Software contract: sqrt function requires non-negative input
Library checkout system with borrowing rules
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Two-party contract diagram showing obligations and benefits for client and supplier

subsections.title: DbC Principles and Benefits
keyPoints: Principle 1: Separate concerns (what vs. how)
Principle 2: Make contracts explicit and checkable
Principle 3: Fail fast when contracts are violated
Benefits: documentation, debugging, testing, reliability, reusability
DbC as a design methodology, not just an implementation technique
examples: Self-documenting code through contracts
Automatic test oracle generation from postconditions
Contract-based component composition
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Mind map showing DbC principles and their benefits radiating outward

exercises: Identify implicit contracts in existing code snippets
Discuss scenarios where contracts would have prevented real-world software failures
Compare DbC with defensive programming approaches

sections.title: Preconditions: Specifying Client Obligations
learningGoals: Define and write effective preconditions
Understand when and how to check preconditions
Apply preconditions to prevent invalid operations

subsections.title: What Are Preconditions?
keyPoints: Preconditions define the valid states for calling a routine
Express constraints on arguments and object state
Client responsibility: ensure precondition before calling
Supplier right: assume precondition holds (no defensive checks needed)
Syntax: require clause in Eiffel, @requires in JML, assert at method start
examples: Stack.pop requires not stack.is_empty
Array access requires valid index: 0 <= i < array.length
Bank withdrawal requires balance >= amount and amount > 0
File operations require file.is_open
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Flowchart showing precondition check before method execution

subsections.title: Writing Effective Preconditions
keyPoints: Be precise: use boolean expressions, not natural language
Be complete: cover all necessary conditions
Be minimal: don't over-specify (allow maximum flexibility)
Use pure expressions: no side effects in contract clauses
Consider both argument validity and object state
examples: Good: require x > 0 and y > 0
Bad: require x is positive (ambiguous)
Over-specified: require x == 5 (too restrictive when x > 0 suffices)
Side-effect error: require list.remove(item) (modifies state)
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Code comparison showing weak vs. strong preconditions with examples

subsections.title: Precondition Violations and Error Handling
keyPoints: Precondition violation indicates client error (bug in caller)
Should not be caught and handled (unlike exceptions)
Fail fast: detect violations as early as possible
Runtime monitoring: enable during development, optionally disable in production
Clear error messages help identify the faulty caller
examples: Assertion failure with stack trace pointing to caller
Precondition violation in sqrt(-1) caught during testing
Production deployment strategies: monitoring levels
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Sequence diagram showing precondition violation detection and program termination

exercises: Write preconditions for common data structure operations (insert, delete, search)
Identify missing preconditions in buggy code examples
Debate: Should preconditions be checked in production code?

sections.title: Postconditions: Guaranteeing Results
learningGoals: Define and write comprehensive postconditions
Use postconditions to specify method behavior
Understand the relationship between postconditions and correctness

subsections.title: Postcondition Fundamentals
keyPoints: Postconditions specify what must be true after routine execution
Express guarantees about return values and state changes
Supplier responsibility: establish postcondition
Client benefit: rely on postcondition without inspecting implementation
Syntax: ensure clause in Eiffel, @ensures in JML
examples: Stack.push(x) ensures not is_empty and top = x
List.sort ensures is_sorted and same_elements(old list)
Account.deposit(amount) ensures balance = old balance + amount
Search function ensures (result >= 0 implies array[result] = key) and (result = -1 implies key not in array)
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Before/after state diagram showing postcondition satisfaction

subsections.title: The 'old' Keyword and State Comparison
keyPoints: 'old' refers to value at routine entry (pre-state)
Essential for specifying state changes
Captures snapshot of mutable objects
Enables relational postconditions (new vs. old state)
Implementation: runtime stores old values when monitoring enabled
examples: ensure balance = old balance + amount
ensure count = old count + 1
ensure list.has(item) and list.count = old list.count + 1
ensure array is permutation of old array
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Timeline showing pre-state (old values) and post-state with postcondition verification

subsections.title: Complete Behavioral Specification
keyPoints: Postconditions should fully characterize routine behavior
Specify both positive effects (what changes) and frame conditions (what doesn't)
Handle all cases: normal execution and boundary conditions
Combine multiple clauses for complex specifications
Balance completeness with readability
examples: Binary search: ensures (found implies array[result] = key) and (not found implies key not in array)
Queue operations: enqueue/dequeue with count and element preservation
Sorting with stability: ensures is_sorted and preserves_relative_order
Graph algorithms: ensures path_exists implies path_found and path_is_shortest
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Decision tree showing different postcondition clauses for different execution paths

exercises: Write complete postconditions for sorting algorithms
Identify incomplete postconditions and add missing guarantees
Create postconditions that specify both functional and performance properties

sections.title: Class Invariants: Maintaining Object Consistency
learningGoals: Understand the role of class invariants in object-oriented design
Write invariants that capture object consistency constraints
Apply invariant preservation rules across all class methods

subsections.title: Class Invariant Concept
keyPoints: Invariant: property that must hold for all instances at all stable times
Stable time: before and after any public method call (not during execution)
Captures the consistency constraints of the class abstraction
Every public method must preserve the invariant
Constructor must establish the invariant
examples: BankAccount: invariant balance >= 0
Date: invariant 1 <= day <= days_in_month(month, year)

slides.title: Design by Contract: Assertions and Program Correctness

blocks.content: Lecture 4: Design by Contract

**The $370M Question:**

Ariane 5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after launch (1996). Root cause: reused Ariane 4 code assumed velocity ≤ 32,767. Ariane 5's faster trajectory produced velocity = 42,000.

`short encoded = (short) velocity; // overflow!`

Could a single line of code have prevented this?

content.title: Pre-Lecture Challenge
content.prompt: Before we define contracts formally: What single check could have caught this error? Where should it go—in the conversion code or in the caller? What are the trade-offs of each choice? Write your answer (1-2 sentences).
content.deliverable: Proposed check + placement decision with one trade-off

slides.speakerNotes: Open with the Ariane 5 disaster to establish stakes and motivate DbC. Give students 2 minutes to propose a solution before formal contract concepts are introduced—this primes analytical thinking and reveals intuitions about responsibility and error detection. Collect a few responses, then explain that today's lecture provides systematic tools (preconditions, postconditions, invariants) to prevent such failures. This opening applies problem-solving to a real case and sets up the 'evaluate' question of responsibility assignment that recurs throughout DbC.

slides.title: Diagnosing the Ariane 5 Failure

content.title: Apply Contract Analysis
content.prompt: What precondition would have prevented this $370M failure? Write a formal precondition for the conversion method. Then evaluate: Should the client (caller) or supplier (conversion method) be responsible for ensuring this condition? Justify your answer considering reusability and fault localization.
content.deliverable: Precondition specification + responsibility assignment with rationale

slides.speakerNotes: Present the Ariane 5 code scenario and give students 2-3 minutes to work individually or in pairs. They must write a precondition (e.g., 'requires velocity >= 0 && velocity <= 32767') and decide whether it belongs to the conversion method or the caller. Facilitate discussion: placing it in the supplier makes the contract explicit and enables reuse checking; placing it in the client distributes responsibility but risks silent failures. This applies contract reasoning to a real failure and evaluates design trade-offs, addressing the 'apply' and 'evaluate' gaps for the precondition-writing objective.

slides.title: The Contract Metaphor

content.prompt: Create a diagram showing two parties (Client and Supplier) with arrows indicating obligations and benefits. Client side: Obligation: Satisfy Precondition, Benefit: Postcondition Guaranteed. Supplier side: Obligation: Establish Postcondition, Benefit: Assume Precondition. Use contract document icon in center.

content.title: Create & Analyze: Multi-Method Contract Design
content.prompt: Design contracts for a BankAccount class with withdraw(amount) and transfer(toAccount, amount). For each method, write preconditions, postconditions, and one class invariant. Then analyze: How do transfer's contracts compose with withdraw's? If transfer calls withdraw internally, what precondition must transfer enforce? Finally, identify one missing guarantee in this specification: 'transfer postcondition: toAccount.balance increases by amount'—what could go wrong?
content.deliverable: Complete contract specifications, composition analysis, and identified specification gap with fix

slides.speakerNotes: Give students 4-5 minutes to design complete contracts. Expected: withdraw precondition 'amount > 0 && amount <= balance', postcondition 'balance == old balance - amount'; transfer must ensure 'amount <= this.balance' before calling withdraw. Invariant: 'balance >= 0'. Composition insight: transfer's precondition must imply withdraw's. Missing guarantee: specification doesn't ensure atomicity or handle toAccount == this. Discuss how students identified the gap—this create-level activity addresses the missing contract composition analysis and completeness debugging gaps while strengthening invariant practice beyond just preconditions and postconditions.

slides.title: DbC Core Principles

items: Separate specification (what) from implementation (how)
Make contracts explicit and machine-checkable
Fail fast when contracts violated

content.title: Evaluate: DbC vs. Defensive Programming
content.prompt: Compare two approaches for a divide(a, b) method: (A) DbC with precondition 'b ≠ 0', caller must check; (B) Defensive: method checks b and throws exception if zero. Analyze trade-offs: Which localizes bugs faster? Which has better performance? Which is clearer for API users? When would you choose each approach?
content.deliverable: Trade-off analysis and justified recommendation for each approach's appropriate context

slides.speakerNotes: Give students 3-4 minutes to analyze both approaches. Expected insights: DbC localizes caller bugs immediately (fail fast at source), defensive catches at callee (error propagated). DbC avoids redundant checks (performance), defensive is safer for untrusted clients. DbC requires discipline, defensive is forgiving. Guide discussion toward context: DbC for internal modules with trusted callers, defensive for public APIs or security-critical code. This evaluate-level activity addresses the gap in critical analysis of when DbC is appropriate versus alternatives, supporting the evaluate objective about how contracts contribute to reliability.

slides.title: Preconditions: Client Obligations

blocks.content:
Preconditions define valid states for calling a routine—constraints on arguments and object state that the CLIENT must ensure.

**Key Principle:** Client responsibility to ensure; supplier right to assume (no defensive checks). Violations indicate bugs in the caller.

content.title: Apply: Trace Responsibility
content.prompt: Given this buggy code, identify: (1) Which line violates the precondition? (2) Is the bug in the caller or pop()? (3) Rewrite the caller to satisfy the contract. Then analyze: If pop() added if(isEmpty()) throw exception, would that fix the bug or just hide it? Justify your answer using DbC principles.
content.deliverable: Bug location, corrected code, and analysis of why defensive checks mask rather than fix contract violations

slides.speakerNotes: This apply-level activity moves beyond explaining preconditions to analyzing buggy code through the DbC lens. Expected answers: Line with bare pop() violates precondition; bug is in caller (failed to check); fix by adding isEmpty() guard. Key insight: defensive checks in pop() hide the caller's bug—it still violates the contract, just doesn't crash. This reinforces that preconditions shift responsibility and enable fail-fast at the true bug source. Poll students on the defensive check question to surface the common misconception that exception handling fixes contract violations. Connects to slide 4's DbC vs. defensive programming comparison.

slides.title: Practice: Writing Preconditions

blocks.content: Given these method signatures, determine appropriate preconditions. Consider argument validity, object state constraints, and what the CLIENT must guarantee.

content.title: Think-Pair-Share (3 min)
content.instructions: For each method: (1) List all preconditions needed, (2) Justify why each is the caller's responsibility vs. supplier's, (3) Write as formal boolean expressions. Compare with a partner—did you identify the same constraints? Discuss: What happens if preconditions are too weak? Too strong?

slides.speakerNotes: This active learning exercise moves students from seeing examples to writing contracts themselves. Expected answers: removeHighest needs !isEmpty(); multiply needs compatible dimensions (this.cols == other.rows); processLines needs path != null, file exists/readable, maxLines > 0. After pair discussion, poll the class and address common issues: forgetting null checks, confusing preconditions with postconditions, over-specifying. Emphasize the analysis required: why is dimension compatibility a precondition rather than throwing an exception? This supports the 'write and apply' objective at true apply level.

slides.title: Writing Effective Preconditions

items: Precise: boolean expressions, not prose (x > 0, not 'x is positive')
Complete: cover all constraints (nulls, boundaries, state)
Minimal: weakest condition that ensures correctness
Pure: no side effects in contract expressions

content.title: Evaluate & Justify (4 min)
content.instructions: Individually: Choose the best precondition (A/B/C) and write 2-3 sentence justification using the four criteria above. Then pair up: Compare choices. If you disagree, debate using criteria—is one over-specified? Missing constraints? Does it enable maximum reusability while ensuring correctness? Prepare to defend your choice to the class.

slides.speakerNotes: This evaluate-level activity requires students to apply all four criteria simultaneously and make a justified design decision. Expected answer: B is best. A is incomplete (missing amount > 0 allows negative withdrawals). C is over-specified (arbitrary 1000 limit reduces reusability without correctness benefit). During debrief, emphasize trade-offs: stronger preconditions are easier to implement but limit clients. Weaker preconditions increase reusability but may require more complex implementations. This bridges to postconditions next slide and supports the apply-level objective for writing contracts.

slides.title: Postconditions: Supplier Guarantees

blocks.content:
**Postconditions** specify guarantees about return values and state changes—what the supplier promises if preconditions are met.

**Key principle:** Client relies on postcondition without inspecting code. Violations indicate implementation bugs.

content.title: Analyze: Debug Contract Completeness (6 min)
content.instructions: The transfer() postcondition is incomplete. Working in pairs: (1) Identify ALL missing guarantees (what about src.balance? return values from withdraw/deposit? edge cases?). (2) Trace how transfer's precondition must strengthen to satisfy withdraw's precondition—what constraint propagates? (3) Write the complete, minimal postcondition. Deliverable: List of missing guarantees + corrected specification. Be ready to explain how contracts compose through method calls.

slides.speakerNotes: This slide elevates from apply to analyze by introducing contract composition and completeness debugging. The transfer() example requires students to trace precondition propagation (transfer must ensure src.balance >= amount to satisfy withdraw's precondition) and identify missing postcondition guarantees (src balance change, both method success, no exception thrown). This addresses two identified gaps: multi-method contract reasoning and contract completeness analysis. During debrief, emphasize that calling contracted methods creates obligations—the caller's precondition must imply the callee's. Common mistakes: forgetting source account state change, not considering exception cases. This prepares students for 'old' keyword mechanics in slide 9 while building compositional reasoning skills.

slides.title: Postconditions with 'old': Specifying State Changes

content.title: Analyze: Debug & Compose Contracts (7 min)
content.instructions:
**Part 1 (3 min):** Identify ALL missing guarantees in these incomplete postconditions:
```
// ensure: balance == old(balance) - amount
withdraw(double amt)  // What about return value? Exceptions?

// ensure: returns sorted list
merge(List<Integer> a, b)  // Missing element guarantees?
```

**Part 2 (4 min):** Analyze contract propagation:
```
transferFunds(Account src, Account dst, double amt) {
  src.withdraw(amt);  // require: amt > 0 && balance >= amt
  dst.deposit(amt);   // require: amt > 0
}
```
What must transferFunds' precondition guarantee? Write complete pre/postconditions. Pair-share findings.
content.deliverable: List missing guarantees; complete transferFunds specification showing contract composition.

slides.speakerNotes: This slide elevates from apply to analyze by requiring students to debug incomplete specifications and trace contract propagation through method calls—addressing two identified gaps. Part 1 targets completeness analysis: withdraw is missing void return specification and exception cases; merge omits element preservation guarantees. Part 2 addresses multi-method reasoning: transferFunds must ensure src.balance >= amt to satisfy withdraw's precondition, and its postcondition must cover both account state changes. During debrief, emphasize that calling contracted methods creates obligations—the caller inherits callee preconditions. Common mistakes include forgetting exception specifications and source account state changes. This prepares students for systematic completeness checking in slide 10.

slides.title: Complete Behavioral Specification

content.title: Analyze & Debug: Identify Missing Guarantees (6 min)
content.deliverable: List of missing guarantees per method; one complete corrected specification with justification.

slides.speakerNotes: This slide elevates from apply to analyze by requiring systematic debugging of incomplete specifications using the completeness checklist. Part 1 targets gap identification: merge missing element preservation and input relationship; authenticate missing false-case semantics and security properties; remove missing return-value/membership relationship and what happens if item absent. Part 2 requires students to synthesize a complete fix and justify it. During debrief, emphasize common incompleteness patterns: forgetting negative cases, omitting return value semantics, and underspecifying state changes. This directly addresses the contract completeness analysis gap and prepares students for slide 11's invariant design by reinforcing systematic specification thinking.

slides.title: Class Invariants: Designing Object Consistency

blocks.content:
Invariant: A property that must hold for all instances at all stable times (before and after any public method call).

• Captures consistency constraints of the abstraction
• Constructor must establish it; every public method must preserve it
• May be temporarily violated during execution

content.prompt: State diagram showing method execution timeline. Show 'Invariant holds' states before method call and after method completion, with 'Invariant may be violated' during method execution. Use green checkmarks for stable states and yellow caution symbol for execution state.

content.title: Design Challenge
content.description:
Consider a `CircularBuffer` class with fields: `items[]`, `head`, `tail`, `count`, `capacity`.

**Your task:** Write 2-3 invariants that must hold. Consider: What relationships must exist between count, capacity, head, and tail? What constraints ensure the buffer is valid?

Think-pair-share: Draft invariants individually (2 min), compare with neighbor (2 min), discuss common mistakes.

slides.speakerNotes: After explaining invariants conceptually, students apply the concept by designing invariants for a concrete data structure. CircularBuffer requires multiple related invariants (0 <= count <= capacity, head/tail within bounds, count reflects actual items). Common student mistakes: forgetting boundary conditions, not relating all fields, or writing invariants that can't be maintained. During pair discussion, circulate and identify interesting approaches. Follow-up questions: 'How does enqueue preserve your invariants?' 'What preconditions do your invariants imply?' This bridges understanding to application, supporting the 'write and apply invariants' objective.

slides.title: Invariant Preservation Analysis

content.title: Multi-Method Contract Composition
content.description:
**Scenario:** capacity=3, state=[A,B,_], head=0, tail=2, count=2. Execute: `dequeue(); enqueue(C); enqueue(D);`

**Tasks:** (1) Trace all three operations, marking when each invariant holds/violated. (2) Identify the critical moment: after dequeue completes but before enqueue starts—do invariants hold? (3) Design a new method `replace(T item)` that calls dequeue() then enqueue(). What contract must replace() have to preserve all invariants?

3 min individual, then defend your replace() contract to a partner.

slides.speakerNotes: This elevated activity addresses two gaps: multi-method contract reasoning and invariant design practice. Students must trace contract composition across method boundaries—analyzing how dequeue's postcondition enables enqueue's precondition. The replace() design task raises cognitive demand to create-level: students synthesize a new contract by composing existing ones, discovering that replace() inherits dequeue's precondition (count > 0) AND enqueue's precondition (count < capacity), requiring count >= 1. During debrief, ask: 'Can replace() have weaker preconditions than calling dequeue+enqueue separately?' This reveals how contract composition constrains design and connects invariant preservation to method orchestration, supporting both 'write invariants' and 'apply DbC principles' objectives.

slides.title: Assertion Monitoring: Strategy Design Exercise

blocks.content:
**Scenario:** Your team maintains a financial trading system:
• **OrderValidator** (validates trades, ~500 calls/sec, complex invariants checking order consistency)
• **PriceCalculator** (computes prices, ~10K calls/sec, simple null/range preconditions)
• **RiskAnalyzer** (analyzes portfolios, ~50 calls/sec, expensive postconditions verifying regulatory compliance)

Production performance budget: max 8% overhead from assertions.

content.title: Instrumentation & Data-Driven Evaluation
content.description:
**Phase 1 (2 min):** Design monitoring strategy for each component—which assertions (pre/post/invariants) stay enabled in production? Calculate estimated overhead.

**Phase 2 (2 min):** You instrument the system and measure: OrderValidator invariants cost 3% overhead but caught a $2M bug in testing; PriceCalculator preconditions cost 6% overhead; RiskAnalyzer postconditions cost 12% overhead. Revise your strategy with this data. What additional information would make your decision more confident?

**Pair discussion:** Compare initial vs. revised strategies. How did real measurements change your reasoning?

items: Evaluate cost/benefit with actual data, not assumptions
Financial correctness may justify exceeding performance budgets
Consider selective monitoring: disable in PriceCalculator, enable in OrderValidator/RiskAnalyzer
Missing info: bug detection rates, failure costs, audit requirements

slides.speakerNotes: This two-phase exercise raises cognitive demand by adding measurement data that contradicts initial assumptions, forcing students to revise decisions based on evidence—authentic evaluate-level work. Phase 1 establishes baseline reasoning. Phase 2 introduces realistic complications: OrderValidator's high value despite cost, PriceCalculator's prohibitive overhead despite simplicity, RiskAnalyzer exceeding budget. The 'additional information' question pushes toward create-level by having students identify gaps in decision criteria. Debrief should emphasize that real engineering requires iterative refinement as data emerges, and that contracts serve debugging (caught $2M bug), not runtime validation. Connect to next slide's debugging focus by noting violations indicate bugs requiring fixes, not production handling.

slides.title: Contract-Based Debugging

items: Precondition violation → bug in CALLER
Postcondition violation → bug in CALLEE implementation
Invariant violation → bug in CLASS implementation
Contracts provide automatic fault localization

content.title: Multi-Method Contract Debugging
content.description:
**Scenario:** `BankAccount.transfer(amount, toAccount)` calls `this.withdraw(amount)` then `toAccount.deposit(amount)`. During testing, an assertion fails.

**Your task:** For each failure case below, identify (1) which contract failed, (2) which component has the bug, (3) what fix is needed:
• Case A: `withdraw()` precondition fails (insufficient funds)
• Case B: `deposit()` postcondition fails (balance not increased)
• Case C: `transfer()` postcondition fails (total money not conserved)
• Case D: Account invariant fails after `deposit()` (balance became negative)

Trace how contracts compose through the call chain.

items: A: transfer() caller bug—didn't verify sufficient funds
B: deposit() implementation bug—fix method logic
C: transfer() implementation bug—missing rollback on failure
D: deposit() class bug—violated invariant maintenance

slides.speakerNotes: This analyze-level activity addresses the 'multi-method contract reasoning' gap by having students trace contract composition through call chains. Students must distinguish between caller obligations, method implementation bugs, and invariant maintenance failures across three methods. The transfer scenario is realistic and shows how contracts localize faults even in complex interactions. Case C is subtle—postcondition failure in transfer despite withdraw/deposit succeeding suggests atomicity/rollback bug. Case D shows invariant violations can occur even when individual method postconditions pass. Debrief should emphasize that contract violations always indicate bugs requiring fixes, never runtime error handling, connecting to previous slide's debugging-not-validation theme.

slides.title: The Liskov Substitution Principle

blocks.content: Behavioral Subtyping Through Contracts
Objects of a subtype must be substitutable for objects of the supertype without breaking program correctness.

items: Structural compatibility ≠ behavioral compatibility
Contracts formalize LSP: subtypes honor supertype obligations
Violation breaks polymorphism and client assumptions

content.title: Identify LSP Violations
content.instructions: Analyze three inheritance examples: (1) Square extends Rectangle with setWidth() setting both dimensions; (2) ReadOnlyList extends List but throws exception on add(); (3) SortedSet extends Set ensuring iteration order. For each: Does it violate LSP? Why or why not? Which client expectations break? How would contracts expose the violation?

slides.speakerNotes: This analyze-level activity targets the 'Apply contract inheritance rules and understand behavioral subtyping' objective. Students must evaluate whether inheritance hierarchies preserve substitutability by reasoning about behavioral expectations. Square/Rectangle violates LSP because clients expect independent width/height modification—contracts would show postcondition violation. ReadOnlyList clearly violates by strengthening preconditions (add() now requires false). SortedSet doesn't violate LSP—it strengthens postconditions (adds ordering guarantee) which is safe. Guide discussion to connect violations with contract rules from next slide, showing how weakening/strengthening rules prevent these problems.

slides.title: Contract Inheritance Rules

items: Preconditions: may only WEAKEN (require less)
Postconditions: may only STRENGTHEN (promise more)
Invariants: may only STRENGTHEN (add constraints)

content.title: Design Contracted Hierarchy + Analyze Composition
content.instructions: Design a BankAccount hierarchy: (1) Create Account.transfer(to, amt) that calls withdraw() then deposit(). Specify all contracts including invariants (balance constraints). (2) Design PremiumAccount subclass allowing $500 overdraft—write its withdraw() contract. (3) Analyze: when transfer() calls withdraw(), how do preconditions compose? If withdraw() fails its postcondition, what happens to transfer()'s guarantee? (4) Evaluate: does RestrictedAccount.withdraw() requiring amt<=100 violate LSP? Trace through a polymorphic transfer() call to show where substitutability breaks.

slides.speakerNotes: This create/analyze activity addresses multiple gaps: designing complete contracted classes, analyzing contract composition through call chains, and applying inheritance rules. Guide students to see that transfer()'s precondition must satisfy withdraw()'s requirements, and its postcondition depends on both method postconditions holding. PremiumAccount weakens balance>=0 to balance>=-500 (legal). RestrictedAccount's amt<=100 strengthens precondition illegally—polymorphic transfer(500) expects success with Account but fails with RestrictedAccount. Emphasize how composition reveals why inheritance rules matter: violated contracts propagate through call chains, breaking client code that relies on supertype guarantees. Connect to LSP from previous slide and trade-offs in next slide.

slides.title: Evaluating DbC Trade-offs

blocks.content: When Should You Use Design by Contract?
Consider three contexts: (A) Public library API used by thousands of developers, (B) Internal module within a single application, (C) Real-time embedded system with strict performance constraints.

content.title: Critical Analysis Task
content.instructions: For each context, evaluate: (1) Should DbC be used? Why or why not? (2) What are the trade-offs between assertion overhead and safety? (3) How does DbC compare to alternatives like defensive programming, static typing, or formal verification? Justify your recommendations considering reliability needs, performance constraints, and development costs.

items: What happens if contract checking adds 10% runtime overhead?
When should preconditions throw exceptions vs. use assertions?
How do you balance contract specificity with API flexibility?

slides.speakerNotes: This evaluate-level activity addresses the objective 'Evaluate how contracts contribute to program reliability.' Guide discussion toward nuanced analysis: (A) public APIs benefit from clear contracts but might need defensive checks since clients are untrusted; (B) internal modules are ideal for DbC—controlled environment, easier debugging; (C) real-time systems face trade-offs—disable runtime checks in production but use during development. Highlight that DbC isn't universally appropriate—context matters. Emphasize comparing approaches: defensive programming duplicates checks but handles untrusted input; static types catch some errors at compile-time; DbC provides runtime verification with documentation benefits. Push students beyond 'DbC is good' to 'DbC is appropriate when...'

slides.title: Design by Contract: Assertions and Program Correctness

blocks.content: Lecture 4: Design by Contract

**The $370M Question:**

Ariane 5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after launch (1996). Root cause: reused Ariane 4 code assumed velocity ≤ 32,767. Ariane 5's faster trajectory produced velocity = 42,000.

`short encoded = (short) velocity; // overflow!`

Could a single line of code have prevented this?

content.title: Pre-Lecture Challenge
content.prompt: Before we define contracts formally: What single check could have caught this error? Where should it go—in the conversion code or in the caller? What are the trade-offs of each choice? Write your answer (1-2 sentences).
content.deliverable: Proposed check + placement decision with one trade-off

slides.speakerNotes: Open with the Ariane 5 disaster to establish stakes and motivate DbC. Give students 2 minutes to propose a solution before formal contract concepts are introduced—this primes analytical thinking and reveals intuitions about responsibility and error detection. Collect a few responses, then explain that today's lecture provides systematic tools (preconditions, postconditions, invariants) to prevent such failures. This opening applies problem-solving to a real case and sets up the 'evaluate' question of responsibility assignment that recurs throughout DbC.

slides.title: Diagnosing the Ariane 5 Failure

content.title: Apply Contract Analysis
content.prompt: What precondition would have prevented this $370M failure? Write a formal precondition for the conversion method. Then evaluate: Should the client (caller) or supplier (conversion method) be responsible for ensuring this condition? Justify your answer considering reusability and fault localization.
content.deliverable: Precondition specification + responsibility assignment with rationale

slides.speakerNotes: Present the Ariane 5 code scenario and give students 2-3 minutes to work individually or in pairs. They must write a precondition (e.g., 'requires velocity >= 0 && velocity <= 32767') and decide whether it belongs to the conversion method or the caller. Facilitate discussion: placing it in the supplier makes the contract explicit and enables reuse checking; placing it in the client distributes responsibility but risks silent failures. This applies contract reasoning to a real failure and evaluates design trade-offs, addressing the 'apply' and 'evaluate' gaps for the precondition-writing objective.

slides.title: The Contract Metaphor

content.prompt: Create a diagram showing two parties (Client and Supplier) with arrows indicating obligations and benefits. Client side: Obligation: Satisfy Precondition, Benefit: Postcondition Guaranteed. Supplier side: Obligation: Establish Postcondition, Benefit: Assume Precondition. Use contract document icon in center.

content.title: Apply Contract Reasoning
content.prompt: Consider a withdraw(amount) method for a BankAccount class. Write: (1) an appropriate precondition, (2) a postcondition, and (3) identify who is responsible if the precondition fails—client or supplier? Then analyze: if you weaken the precondition to allow any amount, how must the postcondition and implementation change?
content.deliverable: Precondition, postcondition, responsibility assignment, and analysis of weakened contract

slides.speakerNotes: Give students 3-4 minutes to write contracts for withdraw(amount). Expected: precondition 'amount > 0 && amount <= balance', postcondition 'balance == old balance - amount'. Discuss responsibility: client must check precondition before calling. Then analyze weakening: if precondition allows any amount, postcondition must specify exception behavior or partial withdrawal. This applies contract writing to a concrete scenario and analyzes trade-offs between strong preconditions (client burden) versus weak ones (supplier complexity), addressing apply and analyze gaps while supporting the contract-writing objective.

slides.title: DbC Core Principles

items: Separate specification (what) from implementation (how)
Make contracts explicit and machine-checkable
Fail fast when contracts violated

content.title: Evaluate: DbC vs. Defensive Programming
content.prompt: Compare two approaches for a divide(a, b) method: (A) DbC with precondition 'b ≠ 0', caller must check; (B) Defensive: method checks b and throws exception if zero. Analyze trade-offs: Which localizes bugs faster? Which has better performance? Which is clearer for API users? When would you choose each approach?
content.deliverable: Trade-off analysis and justified recommendation for each approach's appropriate context

slides.speakerNotes: Give students 3-4 minutes to analyze both approaches. Expected insights: DbC localizes caller bugs immediately (fail fast at source), defensive catches at callee (error propagated). DbC avoids redundant checks (performance), defensive is safer for untrusted clients. DbC requires discipline, defensive is forgiving. Guide discussion toward context: DbC for internal modules with trusted callers, defensive for public APIs or security-critical code. This evaluate-level activity addresses the gap in critical analysis of when DbC is appropriate versus alternatives, supporting the evaluate objective about how contracts contribute to reliability.

slides.title: Preconditions: Client Obligations

blocks.content: What Must Be True Before Calling?
Preconditions define valid states for calling a routine—constraints on arguments and object state that the CLIENT must ensure.

items: Client responsibility: ensure before calling
Supplier right: assume it holds (no defensive checks)
Violations indicate bugs in the caller

slides.speakerNotes: Preconditions are the entry ticket to a method. Emphasize the responsibility shift: it's the CALLER's job to ensure preconditions, not the callee's job to check them. This is different from defensive programming where every method validates inputs. With DbC, we trust but verify during development. Give the stack.pop example: the precondition 'not is_empty' means the caller must check before calling pop. If violated, the bug is in the caller, not in pop.

slides.title: Practice: Writing Preconditions

blocks.content: Given these method signatures, determine appropriate preconditions. Consider argument validity, object state constraints, and what the CLIENT must guarantee.

content.title: Think-Pair-Share (3 min)
content.instructions: For each method: (1) List all preconditions needed, (2) Justify why each is the caller's responsibility vs. supplier's, (3) Write as formal boolean expressions. Compare with a partner—did you identify the same constraints? Discuss: What happens if preconditions are too weak? Too strong?

slides.speakerNotes: This active learning exercise moves students from seeing examples to writing contracts themselves. Expected answers: removeHighest needs !isEmpty(); multiply needs compatible dimensions (this.cols == other.rows); processLines needs path != null, file exists/readable, maxLines > 0. After pair discussion, poll the class and address common issues: forgetting null checks, confusing preconditions with postconditions, over-specifying. Emphasize the analysis required: why is dimension compatibility a precondition rather than throwing an exception? This supports the 'write and apply' objective at true apply level.

slides.title: Writing Effective Preconditions

blocks.content: Precondition Best Practices

items: Be precise: use boolean expressions, not prose
Be complete: cover all necessary conditions
Be minimal: don't over-specify
Use pure expressions: no side effects

slides.speakerNotes: Quality of preconditions matters. Precision means using formal boolean expressions—'x > 0' not 'x is positive'. Completeness means covering all cases—don't forget null checks or boundary conditions. Minimality is crucial: don't make preconditions stronger than necessary, as this limits reusability. The over-specified example (x == 5) is too restrictive when any positive x would work. Side effects in contracts are forbidden—contracts must be pure observers. Discuss why each bad example is problematic.

slides.title: Postconditions: Supplier Guarantees

blocks.content: What Must Be True After Execution?
Postconditions specify guarantees about return values and state changes—what the SUPPLIER promises to deliver.

items: Supplier responsibility: establish postcondition
Client benefit: rely on guarantee without inspecting code
Violations indicate bugs in the implementation

slides.speakerNotes: Postconditions are the flip side of preconditions—they're what the method promises to achieve. If preconditions are satisfied, postconditions MUST hold after execution. This is the supplier's obligation. Emphasize the client benefit: you can rely on postconditions without reading the implementation. This enables modular reasoning and information hiding. If a postcondition is violated, the bug is in the method implementation, not in the caller.

slides.title: Postconditions with 'old'
slides.speakerNotes: The 'old' keyword is essential for specifying state changes. It captures the value at method entry (pre-state) for comparison with post-state. In deposit, we guarantee the new balance equals the old balance plus the amount—this is a relational postcondition. For push, we specify THREE things: stack is not empty, top element is x, and size increased by 1. Point out how 'old' enables us to express changes precisely. In practice, runtime monitoring systems automatically capture old values when assertions are enabled.

slides.title: Complete Behavioral Specification

blocks.content: Fully Characterizing Method Behavior

slides.speakerNotes: Complete postconditions fully characterize behavior. For binary search, we specify BOTH cases: if found (result >= 0), the element at that index equals the key; if not found (result == -1), the key isn't in the array. For sorting, we need THREE properties: the result is sorted, it's a permutation of the input (same elements), and length is preserved. This completeness is crucial—incomplete postconditions leave behavior underspecified. Ask students: what's missing if we only say 'ensure: isSorted(array)' for sort?

slides.title: Class Invariants: Designing Object Consistency

blocks.content:
Invariant: A property that must hold for all instances at all stable times (before and after any public method call).

• Captures consistency constraints of the abstraction
• Constructor must establish it; every public method must preserve it
• May be temporarily violated during execution

content.prompt: State diagram showing method execution timeline. Show 'Invariant holds' states before method call and after method completion, with 'Invariant may be violated' during method execution. Use green checkmarks for stable states and yellow caution symbol for execution state.

content.title: Design Challenge
content.description:
Consider a `CircularBuffer` class with fields: `items[]`, `head`, `tail`, `count`, `capacity`.

**Your task:** Write 2-3 invariants that must hold. Consider: What relationships must exist between count, capacity, head, and tail? What constraints ensure the buffer is valid?

Think-pair-share: Draft invariants individually (2 min), compare with neighbor (2 min), discuss common mistakes.

slides.speakerNotes: After explaining invariants conceptually, students apply the concept by designing invariants for a concrete data structure. CircularBuffer requires multiple related invariants (0 <= count <= capacity, head/tail within bounds, count reflects actual items). Common student mistakes: forgetting boundary conditions, not relating all fields, or writing invariants that can't be maintained. During pair discussion, circulate and identify interesting approaches. Follow-up questions: 'How does enqueue preserve your invariants?' 'What preconditions do your invariants imply?' This bridges understanding to application, supporting the 'write and apply invariants' objective.

slides.title: Invariant Examples
slides.speakerNotes: Walk through concrete invariants. BankAccount's invariant (balance >= 0) is a business rule—negative balances are invalid. The constructor must establish this from the start. BoundedQueue has a structural invariant: count must be between 0 and capacity. Notice how enqueue's precondition (count < capacity) ensures the invariant won't be violated. Every public method in these classes must preserve their respective invariants. Ask: what happens if we forget to check the invariant after an operation?

slides.title: Assertion Monitoring: Strategy Design Exercise

blocks.content: Analyzing Monitoring Trade-offs

**Scenario:** Your team maintains a financial trading system with these components:
• **OrderValidator** (validates trades, ~500 calls/sec, complex invariants)
• **PriceCalculator** (computes prices, ~10K calls/sec, simple preconditions)
• **RiskAnalyzer** (analyzes portfolios, ~50 calls/sec, expensive postconditions)

Production performance budget: max 8% overhead from assertions.

content.prompt: **Design Task:** For each component, decide which assertions (preconditions/postconditions/invariants) to enable in production and justify your choices. Consider: call frequency, check complexity, bug impact if uncaught. Be prepared to defend your trade-offs.

items: High-frequency + cheap checks → often worth keeping
Low-frequency + expensive checks → evaluate bug severity
Financial correctness → favor safety over performance
Remember: violations indicate BUGS, not recoverable errors

slides.speakerNotes: This exercise elevates from understanding monitoring levels to evaluating trade-offs and applying judgment. Students must analyze frequency vs. cost vs. risk—classic evaluate-level reasoning. After individual work, have pairs compare decisions and justify differences. Debrief by revealing that OrderValidator's invariants caught a $2M bug in testing—would they still disable them? Highlight that PriceCalculator's high frequency makes even cheap checks costly, but preconditions are trivial to verify. This connects to 'use assertions for debugging' objective by requiring strategic application decisions.

slides.title: Contract-Based Debugging

blocks.content: Pinpointing Bugs with Contracts

items: Precondition violation → bug in CALLER
Postcondition violation → bug in CALLEE implementation
Invariant violation → bug in CLASS implementation
Contracts provide automatic fault localization

content.prompt: Flowchart for debugging with contracts. Start with 'Assertion Violation', branch to three paths: 'Precondition?' leads to 'Fix Caller', 'Postcondition?' leads to 'Fix Method Implementation', 'Invariant?' leads to 'Fix Class Logic'. Use different colors for each path.

slides.speakerNotes: Contracts are powerful debugging tools because they automatically identify WHO is responsible for a bug. If a precondition fails, the caller didn't satisfy its obligation—fix the caller. If a postcondition fails, the method didn't deliver its promise—fix the implementation. If an invariant fails, the class logic is broken—fix the class. This is much more efficient than traditional debugging where you might spend hours tracking down which component is faulty. Walk through an example: stack overflow caught by precondition immediately tells you the caller tried to push onto a full stack.

slides.title: The Liskov Substitution Principle

blocks.content: Behavioral Subtyping Through Contracts
Objects of a subtype must be substitutable for objects of the supertype without breaking program correctness.

items: Structural compatibility is not enough
Must preserve behavioral expectations
Contracts formalize LSP requirements
Foundation for safe polymorphism

slides.speakerNotes: LSP is fundamental to object-oriented design. It's not enough for a subclass to have the same method signatures—it must behave correctly when used in place of the superclass. The classic Rectangle/Square problem violates LSP: if Square inherits from Rectangle, setting width and height independently breaks. Contracts make LSP precise: subtypes must honor supertype contracts with clients. This is crucial for polymorphism—you need to safely use a subtype wherever a supertype is expected. DbC provides the formal framework for ensuring LSP compliance.

slides.title: Contract Inheritance Rules

items: Preconditions: may only WEAKEN (require less)
Postconditions: may only STRENGTHEN (promise more)
Invariants: may only STRENGTHEN (add constraints)

slides.speakerNotes: Contract inheritance rules ensure LSP compliance. Weakening preconditions means accepting MORE inputs than the parent—this is safe because clients expect to satisfy the parent's precondition. Strengthening postconditions means promising MORE than the parent—also safe because clients expect at least what the parent promises. The Circle example shows valid strengthening: it guarantees the specific formula while still ensuring area >= 0. The BadCircle shows an invalid strengthening of precondition—clients might call with radius <= 0 expecting it to work per the parent contract. These rules are mathematical: they ensure substitutability.
