gaps: Limited remember-level foundation: The deck jumps immediately into apply/analyze activities (Ariane 5 problem-solving in slide 1) without establishing basic terminology. Students unfamiliar with 'precondition' or 'postcondition' may struggle. Consider adding a brief definitions slide before slide 5.

Uneven create-level distribution: Only 5% create-level content, concentrated in slides 3, 12, and 16. The 'Integrate DbC techniques' objective suggests more synthesis opportunities. Consider adding a capstone activity requiring students to design a complete contracted class from scratch.

Missing explicit connection between assertion monitoring (slides 13-14) and contract inheritance (slides 15-16): These topics are taught separately but interact in practice—how do inherited contracts affect monitoring strategy? A bridging activity could strengthen integration.

Contract completeness analysis is strong (slides 8-10) but could benefit from a systematic checklist or heuristic: Students debug incomplete specifications but aren't given a reusable framework for ensuring completeness in future work.

Limited metacognitive scaffolding: Activities provide strong cognitive engagement but rarely ask students to reflect on their reasoning process (e.g., 'What made this specification hard to complete?' or 'How did you decide which contract to strengthen?'). Metacognitive prompts could deepen learning.
suggestions: Add a brief 'Contract Vocabulary' slide (remember-level) before slide 5 defining precondition, postcondition, invariant, and 'old' keyword with minimal examples. This provides a foundation for students encountering DbC for the first time without disrupting the apply/analyze flow.

Expand slide 16's activity to include a create-level capstone: After designing the BankAccount hierarchy, ask students to design a complete TransactionLog class that observes account operations, specifying all contracts and explaining how it integrates with existing contracts. This would raise create-level content to ~10% and better address the 'integrate DbC techniques' objective.

Add a bridging question to slide 15 or 16: 'How does contract inheritance affect your monitoring strategy from slide 13? If a subclass weakens preconditions, which assertions must remain enabled to catch violations?' This connects two major topics and reinforces compositional reasoning.

Provide a 'Contract Completeness Checklist' in slide 10: (1) All input cases covered? (2) All output cases specified? (3) All state changes documented? (4) Edge cases handled? (5) Return value semantics clear? (6) Exception conditions specified? Students can apply this heuristic in future activities and assignments.

Add metacognitive prompts to 2-3 activities: In slide 7, after evaluating preconditions A/B/C, ask 'What criteria did you prioritize? How would you explain your reasoning to a teammate?' In slide 14, after debugging, ask 'What pattern helped you localize the bug? How could you apply this pattern to other failures?' This builds transferable debugging skills.

Consider adding a 'Common DbC Mistakes' slide (analyze-level) after slide 10: Present 3-4 flawed contracts (e.g., precondition with side effects, postcondition that doesn't use 'old', invariant that can't be maintained) and have students diagnose the errors. This would strengthen error recognition skills and provide formative assessment.

Strengthen the connection between slides 1-2 (Ariane 5) and slide 17 (trade-offs): In slide 17, explicitly revisit Ariane 5 and ask 'Given what we now know, how would you have instrumented the Ariane 4->5 code reuse? What contracts and monitoring strategy would have caught the overflow?' This creates narrative closure and reinforces learning transfer.

Add a peer review component to slide 16's hierarchy design: After students design their BankAccount hierarchy, have them exchange with a partner and critique each other's contracts for LSP compliance, completeness, and inheritance rule adherence. This adds evaluate-level peer assessment and surfaces common misconceptions.

lectures.title: Fundamental Design Patterns I: Creational and Structural Patterns

outline.title: Lecture 5. Fundamental Design Patterns I: Creational and Structural Patterns
outline.summary: This lecture introduces essential design patterns for object creation and structural composition in software engineering. Students will learn the Gang of Four patterns including Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Adapter, Composite, and Decorator. The lecture emphasizes practical application, pattern selection criteria, and real-world implementation strategies within object-oriented systems.
learningObjectives: Understand the purpose and motivation behind design patterns in software construction
Apply creational patterns (Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory) to solve object creation problems
Apply structural patterns (Adapter, Composite, Decorator) to organize class and object composition
Evaluate and select appropriate patterns based on design requirements and trade-offs
Implement design patterns using object-oriented principles including inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation
Recognize design patterns in real-world software systems and frameworks

sections.title: Introduction to Design Patterns
learningGoals: Understand what design patterns are and why they matter
Recognize the historical context and Gang of Four contribution
Identify the three main categories of design patterns

subsections.title: What Are Design Patterns?
keyPoints: Reusable solutions to commonly occurring problems in software design
Not finished code, but templates for solving problems in various contexts
Capture expert knowledge and best practices accumulated over decades
Provide a shared vocabulary for developers to communicate design decisions
Balance between flexibility, reusability, and complexity
examples: Analogy: Architectural patterns in building construction (arches, columns)
Recipe vs. actual meal: pattern vs. implementation
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Conceptual diagram showing problem-pattern-solution relationship

subsections.title: Gang of Four and Pattern Categories
keyPoints: Design Patterns book (1994) by Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides
23 classic patterns organized into three categories
Creational patterns: object creation mechanisms
Structural patterns: object and class composition
Behavioral patterns: object interaction and responsibility (next lecture)
Patterns work together and complement each other
examples: Java Collections Framework uses multiple patterns
GUI frameworks heavily rely on structural and behavioral patterns
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Taxonomy diagram showing the three pattern categories with examples

exercises: Identify potential design problems in a given code snippet that could benefit from patterns
Match common software design problems to appropriate pattern categories

sections.title: Creational Patterns: Singleton
learningGoals: Understand when and why to use Singleton pattern
Implement thread-safe Singleton in object-oriented languages
Recognize the trade-offs and criticisms of Singleton

subsections.title: Singleton Pattern: Intent and Structure
keyPoints: Intent: Ensure a class has only one instance and provide global access point
Use when exactly one object is needed to coordinate actions across system
Private constructor prevents external instantiation
Static method provides controlled access to the single instance
Lazy vs. eager initialization strategies
examples: Configuration manager for application settings
Logger instance shared across application
Database connection pool manager
Device driver for hardware resource
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing Singleton structure with private constructor and getInstance() method

subsections.title: Singleton Implementation and Concerns
keyPoints: Thread-safety issues in multi-threaded environments
Double-checked locking pattern for lazy initialization
Enum-based Singleton in Java (best practice)
Criticisms: global state, testing difficulties, hidden dependencies
Violates Single Responsibility Principle (manages lifecycle + business logic)
Consider alternatives: dependency injection, factory patterns
examples: Thread-safe Singleton implementation in Java and Python
Problems with Singleton in unit testing (mocking difficulties)
Refactoring Singleton to dependency-injected service
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Code comparison showing naive vs. thread-safe Singleton implementations

exercises: Implement a thread-safe Singleton for a configuration manager
Identify problems in a given Singleton implementation
Refactor code using Singleton to use dependency injection instead

sections.title: Creational Patterns: Factory Method
learningGoals: Apply Factory Method to delegate object creation to subclasses
Understand the relationship between Factory Method and polymorphism
Distinguish between Factory Method and simple factory functions

subsections.title: Factory Method Pattern: Intent and Structure
keyPoints: Intent: Define interface for creating objects, let subclasses decide which class to instantiate
Defers instantiation to subclasses through inheritance
Creator class declares factory method returning product type
Concrete creators override factory method to return specific product instances
Promotes loose coupling between creator and concrete products
Follows Open/Closed Principle: open for extension, closed for modification
examples: Document editor creating different document types (Text, Spreadsheet, Presentation)
GUI framework creating platform-specific UI components
Logistics system with different transport methods (Truck, Ship, Plane)
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing Creator-Product hierarchy with factory method

subsections.title: Factory Method in Practice
keyPoints: Template Method pattern often uses Factory Method
Parallel class hierarchies: creators and products
Can use parameters to select product variant within same factory method
Difference from static factory methods (simple factories)
When to use: when class cannot anticipate type of objects to create
Trade-off: requires subclassing, increases number of classes
examples: Java Iterator pattern (Collection.iterator() factory method)
Framework hooks for application-specific object creation
Game engine creating different enemy types based on level
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Sequence diagram showing factory method invocation and object creation flow

exercises: Design a Factory Method solution for a payment processing system with multiple payment types
Extend existing Factory Method implementation to support new product variant
Compare Factory Method vs. direct instantiation in terms of flexibility and complexity

sections.title: Creational Patterns: Abstract Factory
learningGoals: Apply Abstract Factory to create families of related objects
Understand how Abstract Factory ensures product compatibility
Distinguish Abstract Factory from Factory Method

subsections.title: Abstract Factory Pattern: Intent and Structure
keyPoints: Intent: Provide interface for creating families of related/dependent objects without specifying concrete classes
Creates multiple products that are designed to work together
Abstract factory declares creation methods for each product type
Concrete factories implement methods to create specific product variants
Ensures products from same family are used together
Client code works with factories and products through abstract interfaces
examples: UI toolkit creating widgets for different platforms (Windows, macOS, Linux)
Furniture shop creating matching furniture sets (Victorian, Modern, ArtDeco)
Game creating themed environment elements (Medieval, SciFi, Fantasy)
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing Abstract Factory with multiple product families

subsections.title: Abstract Factory vs. Factory Method
keyPoints: Abstract Factory uses object composition, Factory Method uses inheritance
Abstract Factory creates product families, Factory Method creates single products
Abstract Factory often implemented using Factory Methods
Adding new product types requires changing all factory interfaces (limitation)
Adding new product families only requires new concrete factory (strength)
Consider when product variants must be used together consistently
examples: Cross-platform GUI framework ensuring consistent look-and-feel
Database abstraction layer with different SQL dialects and connection types
Document converter supporting multiple input/output format combinations
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Comparison table and diagram showing Factory Method vs. Abstract Factory

exercises: Design Abstract Factory for cross-platform notification system (email, SMS, push)
Extend Abstract Factory to support new product family without modifying existing code
Identify when to use Factory Method vs. Abstract Factory in given scenarios

sections.title: Structural Patterns: Adapter
learningGoals: Apply Adapter pattern to integrate incompatible interfaces
Implement both class and object adapters
Recognize adapter usage in existing frameworks and libraries

subsections.title: Adapter Pattern: Intent and Structure
keyPoints: Intent: Convert interface of class into another interface clients expect
Allows classes with incompatible interfaces to work together
Two variants: Class Adapter (inheritance) and Object Adapter (composition)
Wraps existing class with new interface without modifying original code
Promotes reusability of existing code in new contexts
Also known as Wrapper pattern
examples: Integrating third-party library with different interface than your system expects
Legacy system integration with modern applications
Power adapter analogy: US plug to European socket
Java InputStreamReader adapting InputStream to Reader interface
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing both Class Adapter and Object Adapter structures

subsections.title: Adapter Implementation Strategies
keyPoints: Object Adapter: uses composition, more flexible, can adapt multiple adaptees
Class Adapter: uses multiple inheritance (where supported), more efficient
Two-way adapters allow interface to work in both directions
Adapter can add additional functionality beyond interface conversion
Trade-off: adds indirection layer, slight performance overhead
Consider when: cannot modify existing code, need to use several existing subclasses
examples: Adapting legacy Rectangle class to modern Shape interface
Database driver adapters for different DBMS vendors
Media player adapter supporting various audio formats
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Code example showing Object Adapter implementation with delegation

exercises: Implement adapter to integrate third-party logging library with your application's logger interface
Design two-way adapter for bidirectional communication between incompatible systems
Identify adapters in Java Collections Framework or other standard libraries

sections.title: Structural Patterns: Composite
learningGoals: Apply Composite pattern to represent part-whole hierarchies
Implement tree structures with uniform treatment of individual and composite objects
Understand recursive composition and its applications

subsections.title: Composite Pattern: Intent and Structure
keyPoints: Intent: Compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies
Lets clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly
Component interface defines operations for both leaf and composite objects
Leaf represents primitive objects with no children
Composite stores child components and implements child-related operations
Recursive composition: composites can contain other composites
examples: File system: files and directories (directories contain files and other directories)
GUI components: containers and widgets (panels contain buttons, labels, other panels)
Organization hierarchy: employees and departments
Graphic drawing: shapes and groups of shapes
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing Component-Leaf-Composite structure with tree visualization

subsections.title: Composite Pattern Implementation
keyPoints: Transparency vs. safety trade-off in component interface design
Transparent: child management in Component (uniform but unsafe for leaves)
Safe: child management only in Composite (safe but not uniform)
Parent references for traversing tree upward
Ordering of children may or may not matter
Caching results for performance optimization
Visitor pattern often used with Composite for operations
examples: Menu system with nested menus and menu items
Expression tree for mathematical expressions or compilers
Scene graph in 3D graphics engines
Document structure with sections, paragraphs, and text runs
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Sequence diagram showing recursive operation execution through composite tree

exercises: Implement Composite pattern for file system with size calculation operation
Design organization chart using Composite with salary calculation across hierarchy
Add new operation to existing Composite structure without modifying existing classes

sections.title: Structural Patterns: Decorator
learningGoals: Apply Decorator pattern to add responsibilities dynamically
Understand how Decorator provides flexible alternative to subclassing
Implement decorator chains for combining multiple behaviors

subsections.title: Decorator Pattern: Intent and Structure
keyPoints: Intent: Attach additional responsibilities to object dynamically
Provides flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality
Decorator conforms to interface of component it decorates
Decorator contains reference to component and forwards requests to it
Can add behavior before/after forwarding request
Multiple decorators can be stacked to combine behaviors
examples: Java I/O streams: BufferedInputStream wrapping FileInputStream
GUI components: adding scrollbars, borders to windows
Coffee shop: adding milk, sugar, whipped cream to coffee
Text formatting: adding bold, italic, underline to text
subsections.suggestedDiagram: UML class diagram showing Component-ConcreteComponent-Decorator structure

subsections.title: Decorator vs. Inheritance and Implementation
keyPoints: Decorator adds responsibilities at runtime, inheritance at compile-time
Avoids feature-laden classes high in hierarchy
More flexible than static inheritance: can mix and match decorators
Can apply multiple decorators in different orders
Drawback: many small objects, can complicate debugging
Component interface must be sufficient for all decorators
Decorator is not identical to component (identity issues)
examples: Stream processing pipeline with multiple filters
Middleware chain in web frameworks
Notification system with multiple delivery channels
Data compression and encryption layers
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Object diagram showing decorator chain with multiple decorators wrapping component

exercises: Implement decorator chain for text processing (encryption, compression, encoding)
Design notification system using decorators for different delivery methods
Compare decorator approach vs. inheritance for adding features to a class

sections.title: Pattern Selection and Application
learningGoals: Evaluate design problems to select appropriate patterns
Understand trade-offs and consequences of pattern choices
Recognize when not to use patterns (anti-patterns)

subsections.title: Criteria for Pattern Selection
keyPoints: Identify the design problem and forces at play
Consider flexibility requirements: compile-time vs. runtime
Evaluate coupling and cohesion implications
Assess complexity cost vs. flexibility benefit
Consider team familiarity and maintainability
Multiple patterns may solve same problem differently
Patterns are not always the answer: YAGNI principle
examples: Choosing between Factory Method and Abstract Factory based on product families
Adapter vs. Facade for interface simplification needs
When Singleton is actually appropriate vs. dependency injection
Decorator vs. Strategy for adding behavior
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Decision tree or flowchart for pattern selection based on requirements

subsections.title: Patterns in Real-World Systems
keyPoints: Patterns rarely appear in isolation in real systems
Patterns collaborate and complement each other
Framework design heavily relies on pattern combinations
Recognizing patterns in existing code aids understanding
Refactoring to patterns vs. designing with patterns upfront
Over-engineering risk: applying patterns unnecessarily
Pattern evolution: modern interpretations and variations
examples: Java Collections Framework: Iterator, Factory Method, Composite
Spring Framework: Singleton, Factory, Proxy, Template Method
GUI frameworks: Composite, Decorator, Observer, Strategy
ORM frameworks: Factory, Proxy, Template Method
Refactoring example: evolving simple code to pattern-based design
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Architecture diagram showing multiple patterns working together in a framework

exercises: Analyze given codebase to identify which patterns are used and why
Select appropriate patterns for a new system design scenario with specific requirements
Refactor procedural code to incorporate appropriate design patterns
Critique over-engineered code that misuses patterns

sections.title: Summary and Next Steps
learningGoals: Consolidate understanding of creational and structural patterns
Preview behavioral patterns for next lecture
Connect patterns to course learning objectives

subsections.title: Lecture Recap and Integration
keyPoints: Creational patterns: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory control object creation
Structural patterns: Adapter, Composite, Decorator organize object composition
Patterns embody object-oriented principles: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism
Pattern selection depends on specific design forces and trade-offs
Patterns provide vocabulary for design communication
Next lecture: Behavioral patterns (Observer, Strategy, Visitor, Template Method)
Connection to ILO 4: Apply fundamental design patterns
examples: How patterns support Design by Contract (ILO 3)
Patterns enabling high-quality, extendible, reusable systems
Preparation for advanced patterns in later modules
subsections.suggestedDiagram: Summary matrix showing all covered patterns with intent and key characteristics

exercises: Complete tutorial exercises implementing each pattern
Prepare for next lecture by reading about Observer and Strategy patterns
Portfolio assignment: Design small system using at least three patterns from this lecture

suggestedResources: Gamma, E., Helm, R., Johnson, R., & Vlissides, J. (1994). Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software. Addison-Wesley.
Freeman, E., & Freeman, E. (2004). Head First Design Patterns. O'Reilly Media.

Code review exercise: Identify patterns in provided codebase and suggest improvements
Design critique: Evaluate given design and recommend appropriate patterns to address identified issues
Pattern selection quiz: Given scenarios, select most appropriate pattern with reasoning
Refactoring exercise: Transform procedural code to pattern-based object-oriented design

Written examination questions on pattern intent, structure, and application (aligns with 50% written exam)

slides.title: Fundamental Design Patterns I: Creational and Structural Patterns

blocks.content: Lecture 5: Fundamental Design Patterns I
Creational and Structural Patterns

content.title: Design Challenge Preview
content.instructions: Scenario: You're building a document editor that needs multiple file format exporters (PDF, HTML, XML) and must add features like spell-check and auto-save to documents dynamically. Sketch one approach to organize this code. What design problems do you anticipate?
content.format: Individual brainstorm (1 min), then share one challenge with neighbor (1 min). We'll revisit solutions using today's patterns.

slides.speakerNotes: Open with an authentic design challenge requiring both object creation (exporters) and composition (dynamic features). Students apply prior OO knowledge to sketch solutions, surfacing problems patterns will solve: proliferating classes, inflexible instantiation, tight coupling. This primes analyze-level thinking about design forces. Collect 2-3 anticipated challenges via volunteers. Emphasize we'll return to this scenario after learning patterns, creating a throughline for evaluating pattern selection and combination. This transforms a passive title slide into active problem framing.

slides.title: What Are Design Patterns?

blocks.content: Reusable solutions to commonly occurring problems in software design—templates capturing expert knowledge, not finished code. Patterns provide shared vocabulary and leverage OO principles (encapsulation, polymorphism, composition).

content.title: Recognize Patterns in Real Code
content.instructions: Examine these Java framework examples: (1) Collections.unmodifiableList(list) wraps a list to prevent modification. (2) Calendar.getInstance() returns platform-specific calendar implementations. Identify which design pattern each uses. Cite structural evidence (wrapping behavior? factory method?) and analyze why the framework designers chose this pattern for each scenario.
content.format: Individual analysis (1.5 min), pair comparison (1 min), poll with reasoning (0.5 min)

content.title: Create Pattern Combination
content.instructions: Design a notification system where messages can be sent via Email, SMS, or Push, and you need to add encryption and logging dynamically to any combination. Propose which 2-3 patterns to combine, sketch how they collaborate (class relationships), and justify why this design handles future notification types and feature additions better than inheritance hierarchies.
content.format: Individual design sketch (2 min), share with neighbor and critique each other's approach (2 min)

slides.speakerNotes: Strengthen pattern recognition (objective 6) and create-level synthesis before formal pattern introduction. First activity engages analyze-level pattern identification in real frameworks (unmodifiableList is Decorator, getInstance is Factory Method), building recognition skills across authentic code. Second activity elevates to create level: students synthesize multiple patterns into novel architecture, requiring them to generate solutions rather than evaluate pre-defined options. This addresses the deck's 2% create-level gap. Collect diverse designs to show multiple valid pattern combinations (e.g., Factory + Decorator, Strategy + Decorator), emphasizing context-dependent selection—priming evaluation skills for later comparative activities.

slides.title: Pattern Categories: Analyzing Design Intent

content.prompt: Hierarchical diagram with three colored boxes: 'Creational Patterns' (blue) showing Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory with 'Controls object creation'; 'Structural Patterns' (green) showing Adapter, Composite, Decorator with 'Organizes object composition'; 'Behavioral Patterns' (gray) with 'Next Lecture' label. Include design intent labels under each category.

content.title: Framework Pattern Recognition & Synthesis
content.instructions: Part 1 (2 min): Examine real framework code: (a) Spring's BeanFactory.getBean() returns configured objects; (b) Java's Arrays.asList() wraps arrays as lists; (c) File system hierarchies treating files and folders uniformly. Identify the pattern category for each, citing structural evidence. Part 2 (3 min): Design a plugin system where plugins are loaded dynamically and can have logging/security added at runtime. Propose 2+ pattern categories to combine and sketch how they collaborate.
content.format: Individual analysis (2 min), pair synthesis and critique (3 min)

slides.speakerNotes: Gang of Four organized 23 patterns by design intent: creational (object creation), structural (composition), behavioral (interaction). This activity elevates cognitive demand: Part 1 strengthens pattern recognition (objective 6) through real framework analysis—BeanFactory is creational (Abstract Factory), asList is structural (Adapter), file systems use structural (Composite). Part 2 engages create-level synthesis, addressing the deck's 2% create gap: students must generate novel multi-pattern architectures rather than selecting from given options. Collect diverse plugin designs showing Factory+Decorator, Abstract Factory+Composite combinations, emphasizing context-dependent pattern selection.

slides.title: Singleton Pattern: Ensuring One Instance

content.prompt: UML class diagram showing Singleton class with private static instance variable, private constructor marked '-Singleton()', public static getInstance() method returning Singleton type. Show self-reference arrow from getInstance to instance. Add note box: 'Controls instantiation through static method and private constructor.'

content.title: Apply & Analyze Singleton
content.instructions: Implement a ThreadPoolManager Singleton with: (1) private constructor initializing 10 worker threads, (2) getInstance() method, (3) getAvailableThread() method. Then analyze: Why is Singleton appropriate here? What problems arise if multiple ThreadPoolManager instances existed? How would you test this class?
content.format: Individual coding (2 min), pair analysis (2 min)

items: Intent: Exactly one instance, global access point
Mechanism: Private constructor + static accessor
Use when: Coordinating shared resources (configs, pools, caches)
Trade-off: Testability vs. controlled instantiation

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates from understand to apply/analyze. Students implement Singleton mechanism (apply objective 3), then analyze appropriateness for resource coordination—multiple thread pools would cause resource conflicts and inconsistent state. During pair discussions, listen for testing challenges: global state prevents mocking, hard to reset between tests. Probe: 'How does dependency injection address these issues?' Collect 2-3 implementations showing eager vs. lazy initialization strategies. Transition to slide 5's thread-safe implementation examining the volatile double-check pattern.

slides.title: Singleton Implementation: Analyze & Redesign

content.title: Analyze Flaws, Create Alternative
content.instructions: Part 1 (2 min): Analyze why volatile is essential and identify two specific testing problems this creates. Part 2 (3 min): Redesign ConfigManager using dependency injection instead of Singleton. Your design must support: easy unit testing with mock configs, multiple configurations in integration tests. Compare your solution's trade-offs (testability, complexity, global access) against the Singleton approach. When is each justified?
content.format: Individual analysis (2 min), pair redesign & comparison (3 min)

items: Analyze: volatile prevents partial construction visibility across threads
Create: DI alternative enables constructor injection of configs
Evaluate: Singleton = simple global access; DI = testable but needs container
Context matters: Desktop app config vs. microservice shared state

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates from analyze to create by requiring students to design an alternative implementation, not just critique the existing one. During Part 1, confirm understanding of volatile and testing issues (can't mock, global state persists). Part 2 pushes create-level: students must synthesize DI pattern knowledge to produce testable design. Listen for trade-off justifications—DI wins for testing but adds framework dependency; Singleton appropriate for truly global, stable resources. Collect 2-3 DI implementations showing constructor vs. setter injection. Emphasize recognizing when NOT to use patterns is critical design skill. Transition to Factory Method's controlled instantiation approach.

slides.title: Factory Method: Create & Evaluate Solutions

content.title: Design, Implement & Justify Pattern Choice
content.instructions: Notification system needs Email, SMS, Push alerts based on user preference. (1) Design your own solution using any pattern approach—sketch class structure (2 min). (2) Implement factory method for one notification type in pseudocode (2 min). (3) Compare your design against Factory Method and Simple Factory alternatives: Which best supports adding Slack next month? Which simplifies testing? Justify your final selection with specific trade-offs addressing extensibility, complexity, and team context.
content.format: Individual design/implementation, then trio comparison and justified selection

content.prompt: UML comparing Factory Method pattern (Creator hierarchy with EmailNotifier, SMSNotifier subclasses) versus Simple Factory (single NotificationFactory with switch). Highlight modification points when adding new notification types.

items: Create: Design solution before seeing alternatives—tests synthesis ability
Analyze: Does your approach violate Open/Closed when extending?
Evaluate: Compare complexity vs. extensibility across all three designs
Justify: Optimal choice depends on change frequency and team constraints

slides.speakerNotes: This redesign elevates from evaluate-only to create-then-evaluate, addressing the deck's 2% create-level gap. Students first synthesize their own solution before comparing against standard patterns, revealing whether they can generate viable alternatives independently. During trio discussions, push beyond 'Factory Method is better' to context-dependent justification—Simple Factory may suffice for stable requirements; custom approaches might optimize for specific constraints. Challenge defenses with scenarios: What if notification types change weekly? What if team is unfamiliar with inheritance hierarchies? Collect 2-3 student designs showing novel approaches, demonstrating multiple valid solutions exist. This strengthens objective 4's evaluate competency while engaging create-level synthesis missing from current deck.

slides.title: Factory Method: Create, Apply & Evaluate

content.title: Design Novel Solution, Then Compare Patterns
content.instructions: Payment system needs Credit Card support added to existing Cash payments. (1) CREATE your own extensible design without using named patterns—sketch class structure showing how to add payment types (2 min). (2) APPLY Factory Method to implement CreditCardPayment creation (2 min). (3) EVALUATE all three approaches: your design, Factory Method, and static factory with switch. Which best supports adding PayPal next month while keeping ProcessPayment logic unchanged? Justify selection for: (a) 10 payment types expected, (b) only 3 types ever needed.
content.format: Individual creation/implementation, then trio comparison with context-dependent justification

items: CREATE: Generate solution before seeing patterns—reveals synthesis ability
ANALYZE: Does your design violate Open/Closed when extending?
EVALUATE: Compare modification points, testing isolation across all three
JUSTIFY: Optimal choice depends on change frequency, not pattern popularity

slides.speakerNotes: This slide addresses the 2% create-level gap by requiring students to synthesize their own extensible design before applying Factory Method, revealing whether they can independently generate viable alternatives. During trio discussions, push beyond pattern preference to context-dependent justification—static factory may suffice for stable requirements; novel designs might optimize for specific constraints. Challenge: 'What if payment types change weekly vs. annually?' Collect 2-3 student designs showing diverse approaches. This engages create-level synthesis while maintaining evaluate-level pattern comparison, strengthening objectives 4 and 6 through comparative analysis of student-generated vs. canonical solutions.

slides.title: Abstract Factory: Creating Product Families

content.title: Implement Product Families
content.instructions: Build DocumentFactory creating Parser and ImageExtractor families for PDF and Word formats. (1) IMPLEMENT: Code AbstractFactory interface with createParser() and createExtractor() methods, then PDFFactory and WordFactory concrete implementations (3 min). (2) EXTEND: Add RTFFactory supporting RTF format (2 min). (3) ANALYZE: What code changed when adding RTF? Compare to adding a new product type (FontRenderer) across all factories.
content.deliverable: Working factory code showing family extension vs. product extension trade-offs

items: ANALYZE: Which is easier—adding RTF family or adding FontRenderer product? Why?
EVALUATE: When does family consistency justify Abstract Factory's product-extension cost?
Products must work together (PDF parser + PDF extractor, not mixed)

slides.speakerNotes: This activity provides apply-level implementation practice for Abstract Factory, balancing hands-on coding across all creational patterns per gap analysis. Students implement the factory interface and two concrete families, then extend with RTF to experience easy family addition. The analysis phase reveals Abstract Factory's core trade-off: simple family extension but difficult product-type addition (adding FontRenderer requires changing all factories). During debrief, contrast with Factory Method's opposite trade-off. Collect examples showing students recognized when family consistency requirements justify this design choice, strengthening pattern selection skills.

slides.title: Abstract Factory vs Factory Method: Pattern Selection

content.title: Implement & Justify Pattern Choice
content.instructions: Document editor needs PDF and Word support. Each format requires Parser and ImageExtractor working together. (1) IMPLEMENT: Code AbstractFactory with createParser() and createExtractor(), plus PDFFactory and WordFactory (4 min). (2) EXTEND: Add RTF format support (1 min). (3) CREATE: Propose alternative using Factory Method for parsers and extractors separately. (4) EVALUATE: Compare both designs—which better handles adding formats vs. adding new product types like FontRenderer? Justify final choice.
content.deliverable: Working code for both approaches with justified selection based on extensibility trade-offs

slides.speakerNotes: This activity balances apply-level implementation with create-level design synthesis and evaluate-level justification. Students implement Abstract Factory experiencing easy family extension (RTF), then design an alternative using separate Factory Methods. The comparison reveals Abstract Factory's strength (family consistency) versus its weakness (hard to add product types). During debrief, emphasize when family cohesion requirements justify Abstract Factory's constraints. This addresses the gap in Abstract Factory hands-on practice while engaging create-level by requiring students to generate and compare alternative designs rather than selecting from pre-defined options.

slides.title: Adapter Pattern: Interface Conversion

items: Intent: Convert incompatible interfaces
Wraps existing class with new interface
Two variants: Class and Object Adapter
Enables reuse without modification

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Client using Target interface, Adapter implementing Target and containing Adaptee reference, and Adaptee class with incompatible interface. Show delegation arrow from Adapter to Adaptee with 'adaptee.specificRequest()' label.

slides.speakerNotes: Adapter makes incompatible interfaces work together—like a power adapter converting US plug to European socket. The Adapter implements the interface the client expects (Target) and wraps the existing class (Adaptee). Object Adapter uses composition (shown here)—more flexible, can adapt multiple adaptees. Class Adapter uses multiple inheritance—more efficient but less flexible. Real example: Java's InputStreamReader adapts byte streams to character streams. Use when you can't modify existing code but need it to work with new interface.

slides.title: Adapter Pattern: Evaluate & Create Solutions

content.text:
**Design Challenge**: Your system uses `Logger` interface with `log(String msg)`. A third-party library provides `AdvancedLogger` with `writeLog(String msg, LogLevel level, Timestamp time)`. You need structured logging but can't modify either interface.

**Competing Solutions**: (1) Adapter with hardcoded defaults, (2) Adapter parsing message for level hints, (3) Wrapper adding setLevel() method, (4) Abandon Logger interface entirely.

**Your Task**: Evaluate which solution best fits if clients need occasional level control but mostly default INFO logging.

content.instructions: 1. Individually: Rank the 4 solutions by appropriateness. Justify using OO principles (encapsulation, LSP) and pattern intent (1.5 min). 2. Pair: Compare rankings—what criteria drove your decisions? Identify where solutions violate Adapter pattern vs. becoming different patterns (1.5 min). 3. Create: Propose hybrid solution combining strengths of top 2 approaches (1 min).

slides.speakerNotes: This evaluate-level activity requires students to compare competing solutions against pattern intent and OO principles, not just implement one approach. Key insight: solution 3 violates Adapter pattern (changes Target interface), solution 4 abandons the constraint. During pair work, surface that parsing (solution 2) breaks encapsulation while defaults (solution 1) lose flexibility. The create phase scaffolds synthesis: best hybrid often adds optional configuration to adapter constructor while maintaining Logger interface. Debrief connects to objective 4—pattern selection requires evaluating trade-offs across multiple candidate solutions, not just analyzing one pattern's limitations. Emphasize when to adapt vs. when constraint itself is wrong.

slides.title: Composite Pattern: Part-Whole Hierarchies

items: Intent: Compose objects into tree structures
Treat individual and composite objects uniformly
Recursive composition
Component, Leaf, Composite roles

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Component interface with operation(), Leaf implementing Component, and Composite implementing Component with children list and add/remove methods. Show tree structure with Composite containing both Leaf and other Composite objects.

slides.speakerNotes: Composite represents part-whole hierarchies as trees. Classic example: file system with files (leaves) and directories (composites containing files and other directories). The key insight: clients treat leaves and composites uniformly through Component interface. Composite stores children and delegates operations to them recursively. This enables building complex structures from simple parts. The pattern embodies recursion—composites can contain other composites. GUI frameworks use this extensively: panels contain buttons, labels, and other panels.

slides.title: Composite Pattern: Implementation Challenge

content.title: Apply & Analyze (3 min)
content.instructions:
1. Complete the draw() method using recursive delegation
2. Decide: Should add/remove methods be in Graphic interface or only CompositeGraphic?
3. Justify your choice: What are the trade-offs?

Consider: What happens if client calls add() on a Circle?
content.deliverable: Code completion + design decision with rationale

slides.speakerNotes: This active learning exercise elevates engagement to apply and analyze levels. Students first apply the pattern by implementing recursive delegation, then analyze the transparency vs. safety trade-off. Poll students on their interface decision. Transparency (add/remove in Graphic) treats all objects uniformly but allows unsafe operations on leaves. Safety (add/remove only in Composite) prevents errors but requires type checking. Discuss how different contexts favor different approaches: GUI frameworks often choose transparency, while type-safe systems prefer safety. Connect to real design decisions they'll face.

slides.title: Decorator Pattern: Dynamic Responsibilities

items: Intent: Add responsibilities dynamically
Flexible alternative to subclassing
Decorator wraps component
Multiple decorators can be stacked

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Component interface, ConcreteComponent implementing it, Decorator implementing Component and containing Component reference, ConcreteDecoratorA and ConcreteDecoratorB extending Decorator. Show wrapping relationship with nested boxes visualization.

slides.speakerNotes: Decorator adds behavior to objects dynamically without subclassing. Decorator implements same interface as component it wraps and contains reference to component. It forwards requests to wrapped component, adding behavior before/after. Multiple decorators can be chained. Classic example: Java I/O streams—BufferedInputStream wraps FileInputStream, which might wrap another stream. Coffee shop analogy: plain coffee decorated with milk, sugar, whipped cream. Each decorator adds cost and functionality.

slides.title: Decorator Implementation: Design Challenge

content.title: Apply: Complete the Decorator
content.instructions: Implement CompressionDecorator following the pattern structure. Then answer: How would you stack EncryptionDecorator and CompressionDecorator? Which order (compress-then-encrypt or encrypt-then-compress) and why? Consider data size and security implications.
content.deliverable: Sketch class structure; justify decorator ordering with rationale

items: When would Decorator be better than subclassing?
What problems arise with too many decorators?
How does order affect behavior and performance?

slides.speakerNotes: Students implement CompressionDecorator applying pattern structure from slide 14, then evaluate decorator ordering trade-offs. Compression-then-encryption reduces encrypted data size but encryption-then-compression may leak information through compression ratios. Discuss when Decorator beats inheritance (runtime flexibility, avoiding class explosion) versus drawbacks (debugging complexity, many small objects, identity issues). Poll students on ordering choice before revealing that security typically trumps efficiency. This bridges apply (implementation) and evaluate (justify ordering) levels, directly supporting objectives requiring pattern application and selection based on trade-offs.

slides.title: Pattern Selection: Apply the Criteria

content.title: Design Challenge
content.description: You need to add logging to 15+ classes in a legacy system. Logs must include timestamps, user context, and be filterable by severity. Requirements may change (add encryption, remote logging).
content.question: Which approach and why?
options: B. Decorator: Wrap objects with LoggingDecorator
C. Proxy: Create logging proxies for each class

content.title: Evaluate: Justify Your Pattern Choice
content.instructions: Select approach A, B, or C. Apply selection criteria: runtime flexibility needs, coupling impact, extensibility for new features (encryption, remote logging), and maintenance complexity. Justify your choice against the alternatives, identifying which criteria matter most for this scenario.
content.deliverable: Written justification citing at least 3 criteria; explain why rejected alternatives fail

items: Runtime flexibility: Can behavior change without recompilation?
Extensibility: How easily can new features stack?
Coupling: Does solution force dependencies on existing classes?
Complexity vs. benefit: Is added abstraction justified?

slides.speakerNotes: Students evaluate three competing solutions using explicit criteria. Inheritance creates tight coupling, limits runtime changes, and doesn't support stacking features. Proxy requires creating 15+ proxy classes, high maintenance cost. Decorator offers runtime composition, supports stacking (logging + encryption), minimal coupling, but adds object overhead. Poll class on choices before discussion. Reveal that Decorator best fits extensibility and runtime flexibility needs despite complexity. Emphasize trade-off thinking: no perfect answer, but justified selection based on prioritized criteria. This directly targets objective 4 (evaluate and select) at evaluate level, moving beyond conceptual criteria to applied decision-making.

slides.title: Pattern Recognition in Real Systems

content.title: Identify Patterns and Analyze Collaboration
content.instructions: Examine the code. Identify at least 3 patterns used. For each: name the pattern, cite specific evidence (lines/methods), and explain how patterns collaborate. Then evaluate: which pattern could be eliminated if requirements simplified to single logger type? Justify your answer.
content.deliverable: List of patterns with evidence; analysis of how they work together; justified evaluation of which is least essential

items: Patterns: Singleton (WebApp instance), Abstract/Factory Method (LoggerFactory), Decorator (wrapping loggers)
Collaboration: Singleton manages factory; factory creates objects for Decorator chain
Recognition skill: Identify patterns in unfamiliar codebases to understand architecture faster

slides.speakerNotes: Students analyze real code to identify patterns and their interactions—moving from understanding examples to analyzing unfamiliar implementations. Code shows Singleton (getInstance), Factory Method (createLogger/logFactory), Decorator (TimestampDecorator wrapping FilterDecorator). Patterns collaborate: Singleton provides single factory instance, factory creates base logger, decorators add behavior dynamically. Evaluation question targets objective 4: which pattern is least essential? Factory could be eliminated if only one logger type exists, but Singleton and Decorator provide distinct value. Poll students, discuss justifications. This develops pattern recognition in real systems and evaluates appropriateness based on requirements—key professional skills.

slides.title: Summary and Next Steps

blocks.content: Today's Patterns

items: Creational: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory
Structural: Adapter, Composite, Decorator
Patterns embody OO principles: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism
Selection depends on specific forces and trade-offs

blocks.content: Next Lecture: Behavioral Patterns (Observer, Strategy, Visitor, Template Method)

items: Complete tutorial: implement each pattern
Portfolio: design system using 3+ patterns with justification
Read ahead: Observer and Strategy patterns

slides.speakerNotes: Recap: We covered 6 fundamental patterns today. Creational patterns control object creation—Singleton for single instances, Factory Method for subclass-based creation, Abstract Factory for product families. Structural patterns organize composition—Adapter for interface conversion, Composite for tree structures, Decorator for dynamic behavior addition. These patterns embody core OO principles and provide vocabulary for design discussions. Next lecture covers behavioral patterns focusing on object interaction and responsibility distribution. Action items: implement each pattern in tutorial exercises, start portfolio assignment using multiple patterns with written justification, read about Observer and Strategy to prepare. Emphasize connection to ILO 4: applying fundamental design patterns to build high-quality, extendible systems.

slides.title: Fundamental Design Patterns I: Creational and Structural Patterns

blocks.content: Lecture 5: Fundamental Design Patterns I
Creational and Structural Patterns
Mastering Object Creation and Composition

slides.speakerNotes: Welcome to our exploration of design patterns. Today we focus on two categories: creational patterns (how we create objects) and structural patterns (how we compose objects). These are foundational tools that every software engineer should master. Set the stage by emphasizing that patterns are not just academic concepts but practical solutions used daily in industry.

slides.title: What Are Design Patterns?

blocks.content: Reusable solutions to commonly occurring problems in software design

items: Templates, not finished code—adapt to context
Capture decades of expert knowledge
Shared vocabulary for design communication
Balance flexibility, reusability, and complexity

content.title: Pattern Recognition Challenge
content.instructions: Examine this code snippet: A Logger class with a private constructor, static getInstance() method, and single instance variable. What design problem does this solve? What pattern might this be? What trade-offs does this approach introduce?
content.format: Think-pair-share: 1 min individual, 1 min discuss with neighbor, 1 min class discussion

slides.speakerNotes: After presenting the definition and analogy, engage students in analyzing a real pattern implementation before formally introducing patterns. The Logger example is a Singleton (covered in slide 4), but here students diagnose the design intent and trade-offs. This activates analyze-level thinking: identifying the problem being solved, recognizing the solution structure, and evaluating consequences. Use responses to preview that patterns solve specific problems but introduce trade-offs—foreshadowing the evaluation skills needed for pattern selection. Collect answers via polling or volunteers.

slides.title: Pattern Categories: Analyzing Design Intent

content.prompt: Hierarchical diagram with three colored boxes: 'Creational Patterns' (blue) showing Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory with 'Controls object creation'; 'Structural Patterns' (green) showing Adapter, Composite, Decorator with 'Organizes object composition'; 'Behavioral Patterns' (gray) with 'Next Lecture' label. Include design intent labels under each category.

content.title: Pattern Category Diagnosis
content.instructions: Analyze these scenarios and identify which pattern category applies: (1) You need multiple database connection objects to share the same configuration. (2) You want to add logging behavior to existing classes without modifying them. (3) You need a tree structure where individual items and groups are treated uniformly. Justify your category choice based on the design problem.
content.format: Poll responses, then discuss reasoning for each scenario

slides.speakerNotes: The Gang of Four (1994) formalized 23 patterns into three categories based on design intent. Today covers 6 patterns across creational and structural categories. Use the activity to engage analyze-level thinking: students must diagnose the core design problem (object creation vs. composition) and map it to the appropriate category. Scenario 1 is creational (shared creation logic), 2 is structural (adding behavior through composition), 3 is structural (uniform treatment via composition). Collect poll responses and discuss how recognizing design intent guides pattern selection—foreshadowing evaluation skills needed later.

slides.title: Singleton Pattern: Ensuring One Instance

items: Intent: One instance, global access
Private constructor blocks external creation
Static method controls access
Use for coordinating system-wide actions

content.prompt: UML class diagram showing Singleton class with: private static instance variable, private constructor, public static getInstance() method returning the instance. Show the self-reference arrow from getInstance to the instance.

slides.speakerNotes: Singleton ensures exactly one instance exists. Classic examples: configuration manager, logger, connection pool. The key mechanism: private constructor prevents external instantiation, static method provides controlled access. Draw attention to the self-referential nature—the class manages its own unique instance. Mention lazy vs. eager initialization strategies.

slides.title: Singleton Implementation: Design Analysis

content.title: Analyze & Evaluate
content.instructions: Examine this implementation and answer: (1) Why is volatile necessary? What happens without it? (2) Identify one scenario where this Singleton creates problems for testing. (3) Would you use this pattern for a cache manager in a microservices architecture? Justify your answer.
content.format: Think-pair-share: 1 min individual, 1 min pairs, 1 min class discussion

items: ✓ Thread-safe, lazy initialization, low overhead
✗ Hidden dependencies, testing difficulties
✗ Global state complicates distributed systems
Alternative: Dependency injection for testability

slides.speakerNotes: Guide students through analyzing the double-checked locking mechanism—volatile ensures memory visibility preventing partially constructed objects. During activity, listen for: testing issues (mocking difficulties, global state), distributed system concerns (instance per JVM, not truly global). Highlight that pattern choice requires evaluating context: acceptable for desktop app configuration, problematic for distributed cache. Emphasize that recognizing when NOT to use a pattern is as important as knowing how to implement it. Transition to Factory Method as alternative approach to controlled instantiation.

slides.title: Factory Method Pattern: Application & Analysis

content.title: Apply Factory Method
content.instructions: Design problem: You're building a notification system that sends alerts via Email, SMS, or Push. The NotificationService class needs to create the right notifier based on user preferences, but shouldn't depend on concrete notifier classes. Sketch: (1) Which classes/interfaces you'd create, (2) Where the factory method goes, (3) How subclasses provide specific notifiers. Then evaluate: Would simple if-else in one class be better? Why or why not?
content.format: 2 min individual sketch, 2 min pair discussion of trade-offs

content.prompt: UML class diagram showing Creator abstract class with factoryMethod():Product and sendNotification(), ConcreteCreatorEmail/SMS/Push extending Creator, Notifier interface, and EmailNotifier/SMSNotifier/PushNotifier implementing Notifier. Highlight factoryMethod() returns Notifier type.

items: Use when: Creation logic varies by context/subclass
Use when: Framework defines structure, apps provide specifics
Avoid when: Only one product type (over-engineering)
Avoid when: Creation logic simple and stable (use DI instead)

slides.speakerNotes: Guide students through applying Factory Method to notification problem. Listen for correct identification: NotificationService as Creator with createNotifier() factory method, subclasses for each channel. During evaluation, push students to justify: Factory Method adds complexity (parallel hierarchies) but gains extensibility and testability. Simple if-else might suffice for stable requirements, but Factory Method supports Open/Closed when new notification types emerge. Emphasize that pattern choice requires analyzing requirements—stability vs. extensibility, simplicity vs. flexibility. Connect to next slide's logistics example showing similar structure in different domain.

slides.title: Factory Method: Apply & Analyze

content.title: Implement Factory Method
content.instructions: You're extending a logistics system that currently handles Road and Sea transport. Add Air transport support. On paper: (1) Write the AirLogistics subclass with createTransport() method, (2) Sketch the Plane class implementing Transport, (3) Identify which parts you modified vs. extended. Then analyze: What if you had used a simple static factory instead? What would change when adding new transport types?
content.format: 3 min implementation, 2 min pair comparison of Factory Method vs. static factory trade-offs

items: Analyze: Which classes changed? Which were extended?
Compare: Static factory vs. Factory Method for this scenario
Evaluate: Is the parallel hierarchy justified here?
When would simpler approach suffice?

slides.speakerNotes: Guide students through extending the logistics system with Air transport. This apply-level task requires implementing the pattern, not just recognizing it. During analysis, emphasize Open/Closed Principle: adding AirLogistics extends without modifying existing code. Push students to evaluate trade-offs: Factory Method adds complexity through parallel hierarchies but enables extension without modification. Static factory would require modifying existing code for each new type. Connect to slide 6's notification system showing similar extension scenario. Highlight that pattern choice depends on anticipated change—stable requirements favor simplicity, expected growth favors Factory Method.

slides.title: Abstract Factory: Creating Product Families

items: Intent: Create families of related objects
Ensures products work together
Multiple creation methods per factory
Client uses abstract interfaces only

content.prompt: UML diagram showing AbstractFactory interface with createProductA() and createProductB() methods, ConcreteFactory1 and ConcreteFactory2 implementing it, AbstractProductA and AbstractProductB interfaces, and concrete products ProductA1, ProductA2, ProductB1, ProductB2. Use different colors for each product family.

slides.speakerNotes: Abstract Factory creates families of related objects. Key difference from Factory Method: creates multiple product types that must work together. Classic example: UI toolkit creating Button, Checkbox, ScrollBar for Windows/Mac/Linux—products from same family share consistent look. The factory interface declares creation methods for each product type. Concrete factories return compatible products. Client code works only with abstract interfaces, never concrete classes.

slides.title: Abstract Factory vs Factory Method

items: Abstract Factory: object composition, creates product families
Factory Method: inheritance, creates single products
Abstract Factory often uses Factory Methods internally
Adding product types: affects all factories (limitation)
Adding product families: just add new factory (strength)

blocks.content: Use Abstract Factory when products must be used together consistently

slides.speakerNotes: Critical comparison: Factory Method uses inheritance (subclasses decide), Abstract Factory uses composition (factory objects decide). Abstract Factory handles product families—multiple related products. Factory Method handles single product hierarchies. Abstract Factory is often implemented using Factory Methods for each product. Trade-off: adding new product types requires changing all factory interfaces, but adding new product families is easy—just create new concrete factory. Example: adding 'TextField' to UI toolkit requires updating all platform factories.

slides.title: Adapter Pattern: Interface Conversion

items: Intent: Convert incompatible interfaces
Wraps existing class with new interface
Two variants: Class and Object Adapter
Enables reuse without modification

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Client using Target interface, Adapter implementing Target and containing Adaptee reference, and Adaptee class with incompatible interface. Show delegation arrow from Adapter to Adaptee with 'adaptee.specificRequest()' label.

slides.speakerNotes: Adapter makes incompatible interfaces work together—like a power adapter converting US plug to European socket. The Adapter implements the interface the client expects (Target) and wraps the existing class (Adaptee). Object Adapter uses composition (shown here)—more flexible, can adapt multiple adaptees. Class Adapter uses multiple inheritance—more efficient but less flexible. Real example: Java's InputStreamReader adapts byte streams to character streams. Use when you can't modify existing code but need it to work with new interface.

slides.title: Adapter Pattern: Apply & Analyze

content.text:
**Design Challenge**: Your system uses `Logger` interface with `log(String msg)`. A third-party library provides `AdvancedLogger` with `writeLog(String msg, LogLevel level, Timestamp time)`. You need structured logging with levels and timestamps, but can't modify either interface.

**Task**: Design an adapter solution. What goes in the adapter? How does it bridge the interfaces?

content.instructions: 1. Complete the adapter (1 min). 2. Pair: Compare solutions—what assumptions did you make about log level and timestamp? (1 min). 3. Analyze: What are the trade-offs of your design choices? When would this adapter fail? (1 min)

slides.speakerNotes: This apply-level activity has students design an adapter for a realistic scenario. Key learning: adapters often add logic (default LogLevel, current timestamp) beyond simple delegation. During pair discussion, surface different approaches: some hardcode INFO level, others parse message for level indicators. Analysis phase targets evaluate level: trade-offs include loss of caller control over level/timestamp vs. simplicity. Adapter fails if client needs fine-grained control—this reveals pattern limitations. Debrief by showing one solution, then discuss when to use Class Adapter (multiple inheritance) vs. Object Adapter (composition) based on their designs. Connect to objective: applying structural patterns to solve composition problems with justified design choices.

Treat individual and composite objects uniformly
Recursive composition
Component, Leaf, Composite roles

This enables building complex structures from simple parts. The pattern embodies recursion—composites can contain other composites. GUI frameworks use this extensively: panels contain buttons, labels, and other panels.

Flexible alternative to subclassing
Decorator wraps component
Multiple decorators can be stacked

items: When would Decorator be better than subclassing?
What problems arise with too many decorators?
How does order affect behavior and performance?

slides.speakerNotes: Students implement CompressionDecorator applying pattern structure from slide 14, then evaluate decorator ordering trade-offs. Compression-then-encryption reduces encrypted data size but encryption-then-compression may leak information through compression ratios. Discuss when Decorator beats inheritance (runtime flexibility, avoiding class explosion) versus drawbacks (debugging complexity, many small objects, identity issues). Poll students on ordering choice before revealing that security typically trumps efficiency. This bridges apply (implementation) and evaluate (justify ordering) levels, directly supporting objectives requiring pattern application and selection based on trade-offs.

slides.title: Pattern Selection Criteria

items: Identify the design problem and forces
Compile-time vs. runtime flexibility needs
Coupling and cohesion implications
Complexity cost vs. flexibility benefit
Team familiarity and maintainability

blocks.content: Patterns are not always the answer: YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)

slides.speakerNotes: Selecting the right pattern requires analyzing the specific problem. Consider: Do you need compile-time or runtime flexibility? How much coupling can you tolerate? Is the added complexity justified by the flexibility gained? Can your team maintain pattern-based code? Multiple patterns may solve the same problem differently—choose based on trade-offs. Important warning: don't over-engineer. Apply patterns when you have a real problem they solve, not speculatively. YAGNI principle: implement what you need now, not what you might need later. Premature abstraction is as bad as premature optimization.

slides.title: Patterns in Real-World Systems

items: Java Collections: Iterator, Factory Method, Composite
Spring Framework: Singleton, Factory, Proxy, Template Method
GUI Frameworks: Composite, Decorator, Observer, Strategy
Patterns rarely appear in isolation
Refactoring to patterns vs. upfront design

content.prompt: Architecture diagram showing a web application framework with boxes representing different components, labeled with patterns they use: Controller (Factory Method), View (Composite), Model (Observer), Middleware (Decorator), Database (Abstract Factory, Singleton). Show connections between components.

slides.speakerNotes: Real systems use multiple patterns working together. Java Collections Framework: Collection.iterator() is Factory Method, List/Set hierarchies use Composite-like structure. Spring uses Singleton for beans, Factory for bean creation, Proxy for AOP. GUI frameworks are pattern-rich: widget hierarchies (Composite), widget decoration (Decorator), event handling (Observer). Important distinction: refactoring to patterns (evolving simple code as complexity grows) vs. designing with patterns upfront. Fowler advocates refactoring approach—start simple, introduce patterns when needed. Recognize patterns in existing code to understand architecture faster.

slides.title: Summary and Next Steps

blocks.content: Today's Patterns

items: Creational: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory
Structural: Adapter, Composite, Decorator
Patterns embody OO principles: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism
Selection depends on specific forces and trade-offs

slides.speakerNotes: Recap: We covered 6 fundamental patterns today. Creational patterns control object creation—Singleton for single instances, Factory Method for subclass-based creation, Abstract Factory for product families. Structural patterns organize composition—Adapter for interface conversion, Composite for tree structures, Decorator for dynamic behavior addition. These patterns embody core OO principles and provide vocabulary for design discussions. Next lecture covers behavioral patterns focusing on object interaction and responsibility distribution. Action items: implement each pattern in tutorial exercises, start portfolio assignment using multiple patterns with written justification, read about Observer and Strategy to prepare. Emphasize connection to ILO 4: applying fundamental design patterns to build high-quality, extendible systems.
